subsubtopic: TABLING OF THE FOURTH REPORT OF THE STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of tabling, in both official languages, the Fourth Report of the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology respecting centres of excellence.
Today, science and technology have an impact on all sectors of the economy and on all spheres of human endeavor. To adapt to the changes stemming from the applications of science and technology, we must concentrate our efforts on providing quality education at all levels. Furthermore, we must establish and maintain ties between universities and the private sector, where research is carried out.
The centres of excellence program was announced earlier this year with these specific objectives in mind. In view of this program's importance as a means of making Canada more competitive on world markets and since it is a new way for the federal government to fund research activities, the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology wanted to study its provisions closely. In so doing, it wanted to gauge the reaction of those whose primary concern is the quality of research in Canada and to make recommendations with a view to ensuring that the program becomes a major initiative in our drive to enhance our competitive position.
Among other things, the Committee notes in its report that this initiative will go a long way toward ensuring a pool of trained, highly qualified researchers and quality research projects. However, it also states clearly that the centres of excellence program should not be viewed as a substitute for the invaluable research funding provided by the three grant councils.
The Committee believes that ties must be forged between universities and industry to help the latter develop a more innovative approach. This is precisely the goal of this innovative program and the Committee hopes that this report will contribute to the development of truly excellent and successful scientific networks.
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 99(2), the Committee asks the government to provide a comprehensive response to this report.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EQUITABLE TRUCKING AND FREIGHT RATES TO QUEEN CHARLOTTE ISLANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have three petitions to present to the House today. The first one is certified correct pursuant to Standing Order 106 and is from a large number of residents of the Queen Charlotte Islands, from Sandspit, Queen Charlotte City, Masset, Port Clements, and other communities on the Queen Charlotte Islands. They petition Parliament regarding the cost of living on the Queen Charlotte Islands which is already high.
There is a federal subsidy to the ferry to offset its operating costs, but it is not reflected in the freight rates. An example they give is that a 50-pound sack of flour costs $16.50 in Vancouver, whereas once it is shipped to the Queen Charlotte Islands it costs $26.90. Since freight costs have doubled in a year, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure, possibly by reallocation of part of the subsidy, equitable trucking and freight rates to the Queen Charlotte Islands.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition, which has been certified correct pursuant to Standing Order 106, from residents of the Queen Charlotte Islands and other areas. Since the Government, through Bill C-33, seeks to deindex the pensions of federal public servants which now have complete inflation protection through full linkage to the Consumer Price Index and other points, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject Bill C-33 as regressive, unfair, untimely, and against the best interests of public servants and all Canadians, and to affirm full indexing to the Consumer Price Index as the model for inflation protection for all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
that Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to commence debate on the Canada Child Care Act, legislation necessary to implement agreements with the provinces on the expansion of child care services across the country. As Members are aware, this represents a major element of the national strategy on child care which I announced last December. Before I get into the detailed substance of the Bill, I want to talk briefly about our Government's approach to social issues and how the child care strategy relates to this approach.
As a national Government, we are committed to improving opportunities and the quality of life of all Canadians. After all, that is the reason we have a social support system to help people experiencing difficulties, to ensure a basic equity in Canadian society, and to assist people to realize their fullest potential. For any Government addressing social issues and problems it is always difficult. The problems are often complex. The issues are interrelated and opinions on the appropriate way to proceed are usually very divided and quite firmly held. In a country as diverse as Canada, individual lifestyles and values vary considerably even in the same community, and community values may be quite different from one end of the country to the other.
In contributing to the resolution of a social issue, government must always find the proper balance between direct intervention and a laissez-faire approach. If direct intervention seems to be the right answer, government must still ensure that it encourages participation of individuals involved in order that it does not take over the problem or force people to adopt a single solution to that issue. The Government believes very strongly in achieving a balanced approach. We believe that a caring social policy perspective means developing an environment in which people are encouraged to help themselves and in which differing personal and community values are respected. A caring social policy requires thoughtful planning and expertise in its development and a great deal of flexibility in its implementation. That is not new to the child care policy. That, in fact, has been the hallmark of every social policy issue initiative that has been presented in this House throughout the past.
August 11, 1988

Those who feel there are easy answers or those who feel there is only one answer deny not only the present reality but our history. It means working closely with individuals and groups most affected by the issue, recognizing that they can make important contributions to both policy development and the operation of resulting programs. I do not believe any Government is in a position to solve all problems and should never attempt to dictate a single solution to a problem that affects people in different ways.
Another important aspect of our approach to social policy is to focus as much as possible on the future direction of society rather than root our solutions in the past. A good example of this approach is the seniors initiative which my colleague, the Minister of State for Seniors (Mr. Hees), and I announced earlier this year. The initiative concentrates on enhancing health and social services for seniors in a manner designed to maintain both independence and choice for this increasingly significant age group within Canadian society. For example, through the seniors independence program will be funding projects aimed at improving the quality of life and dependence of seniors. Priority is being given to projects involving community groups of seniors and to research activities directed to those diseases most affecting the ability of seniors to function independently.
As in other social policy areas, we believe an effective approach is to put the people most concerned with a problem in charge of developing solutions that work rather than impose solutions from outside the community or from social planners in Ottawa. Where the Government can act to increase the independence of the elderly, such as in the area of more economic self-sufficiency, we have acted as a Government. We have extended the spousal allowance benefits, implemented pension reform, and increased the flexibility of the Canada Pension Plan so that Canadians can make choices with respect to their retirement planning.
Consistent with our focus on the future, we are also assisting Canadians to plan much earlier for financial independence in their retirement years. This has included improving the portability of pensions in the federal sector and encouraging pre-retirement savings through higher RRSP contribution levels and more equitable contribution rights. We have also taken steps to ensure that men and women retiring under similar circumstances have equal pensions. We have also provided for the splitting of pension credits earned during marriages in which divorce occurs.
We have also taken the same approach with respect to health care. Until recently, the sole focus or primary focus of our health care system was to deal with injury and disease, to take an unwell person and make him or her well again. While this will always remain a priority, important new challenges to prevent and where this is not possible to enhance the ability of Canadians to cope better with disease, disabilities and stresses of modern living has become the focus of the health care policy
Canada Child Care Act
of our Government. By promoting more healthy lifestyle choices, we can reduce dependence upon the health care system as well as improve personal quality of life at the same time.
This health promotion strategy also encourages self help and mutual aid practices since it is the community that provides the emotional and practical support to help people make the right choices and to live independently. Over the last few years we have seen the great success of groups addressing alcohol and drug abuse issues. Need I remind Hon. Members who said just a few months ago that there was no drug crisis that they are now seeing the wisdom of the forethought of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he made the announcement of a drugs strategy.
We involved ourselves much more deeply in impaired driving programs. We are finding that teens are taking those programs to heart and are now leading in the development of those programs and in the education of their peers. I need only to mention to the House our strategy on smoking as further evidence of this involvement.
While the Government has instituted national public awareness campaigns and tougher legislation in these areas, community based concern and action have really been responsible for the significant change in public attitude across Canada. One of the more difficult challenges we have responded to is, as I have already mentioned, drug and substance abuse.
Drug dependency claims many victims and can have an absolutely devastating impact on young people, their families, and entire communities. Public awareness can help limit the demand for illicit substances and can bring a hidden activity more into the open, but solving the drug abuse problem requires a deliberate, encompassing and co-ordinated strategy at the local, national, and international levels, including support of innovative community based research and self help.
Like substance abuse, child sexual abuse is a hidden social problem. It has a serious and long-lasting impact on our children, children who in most cases are unable to defend themselves. We are trying to bring the problem into the open, to sensitize communities to the issue, and to soften the impact of the judicial process on children who have been caught up in court proceedings. At the same time, we have severely increased penalties under the Criminal Code for people who abuse the trust that children place in them. However, penalties only deal with the problem after the fact. Improved community awareness and action will ensure that our children are better protected.
Under the pressures of modern life, the Canadian family is undergoing unprecedented changes. There are more single parent families than ever before, more families in which both parents work full time in order to meet their economic obligations, and unfortunately we also see more family breakdown in society.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
As more women participate in the paid labour force or raise children on their own, the need for adequate child care services has become an increasingly pressing. Before I get into the substance of the Bill, I should make the point that the Government is using its data bases to bring responsibility to men especially those who have not taken the responsibility of child support. In some provinces as high as 85 per cent of court orders are either in arrears, are being partially paid, or are not being paid at all. There are many issues to be dealt with as we try to provide policies to improve the society in which we live.
Over the past four years the Government has made a substantial commitment to policies and programs which help Canadian families to deal with these realities. New divorce legislation, better means of enforcing custody and support orders, and a harmonization of federal and provincial efforts in the area of family law are some of the initiatives that have been taken. Programs to deal more effectively with family violence, including the increasing prevalence of abuse of the elderly, are also being worked on in conjunction and cooperation with the provinces.
The national strategy on child care which I was proud to announce on behalf of the Government seven months ago was designed to increase the number of quality subsidized child care spaces that meet the standards parents demand for the care of their children. As I said earlier, the development of an effective, workable social policy is always a difficult endeavour. As is the case with the development of other social programs, individuals have very definite ideas about the extent of the child care problem and about the most effective way to respond. As with other policies, this Government has attempted to bring sensitivity, understanding, and flexibility to bear on developing what I believe to be a very caring national strategy.
While our goal is to increase the affordability, availability, and quality of child care services, we realized that we had to respect the rights of parents to choose the kind of care they thought best for their children. We also had to respect the existing programs and services which provincial governments had developed in response to their own past needs and circumstances. We have also had the advantage of two major task force reports and extensive consultations with interest groups and individual Canadians across Canada. The result, our national strategy on child care, reflects a proper balance of choice, quality and quantity.
While it is a very expensive program-$6.4 billion is the federal commitment alone over the next seven years-it does not place an undue burden on either federal or provincial taxpayers. These are important considerations in developing a policy that is not only workable today but also does not create new problems or burdens for future generations. In fact, in the development of social policy, governments of the past used a similar approach.
As Hon. Members will recall, our strategy consists of four primary components: enhanced tax assistance for families with young children, a new child care initiatives fund, an initiative to stimulate accredited day care for Indian children, and a new federal-provincial cost-sharing program. The first two components are already in place and operating. The Indian
day care initiative is in development, and authority to put the cost-sharing element in place is provided by the legislation we are discussing today.
The details of the components of the strategy have been made public before. Members have had several opportunities to discuss and debate them over the last few months. However, let me reiterate one important point. The supplement to the Child Tax Credit, $100 this year and $200 in subsequent years, is a targeted credit like the child tax credit itself. It goes to low and middle income families where parents remain at home to care for their children or use less formal child care. This tax measure makes up by far the greatest part of the new tax assistance we are making available in the national strategy on child care.
Additionally, it should be remembered that the child tax credit is additional to the increases made in former budgets by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Members should also recall the early prepayment of the enhanced child credit when looking at the entire record of child care. As well, the enhanced child care expense deduction is for those families of whatever income who are using receipted child care arrangements. Under our strategy the deduction more accurately reflects the total cost of child care, thereby reducing the financial burden of child care services. These tax initiatives will be effective this tax year.
The $100 million child care initiatives fund has been designed to support innovative research and demonstration projects to improve and expand child care services. We all know there are many needs which are not now being met by current child care services in systems. Parents who work irregular hours or on shifts, parents in remote or rural areas of Canada, parents of children with special needs, all have requirements for child care services of a different nature than that which the mainstream delivery system provides. The fund will help us develop ways of meeting these kinds of needs so that the quality of services may be improved and all Canadians may have better access to the services they need. This fund has already been established, looks to the future as well as to the present, and involves parents, community groups, and nonprofit organizations in the effort.
The complicated part of the legislation is the new costsharing Bill before us, the Canada Child Care Act, Bill C-144. It is the means through which the federal Government is going to work with the provinces to double the number of child care spaces across Canada over the next seven years. It follows the tradition of consultation that this Government established in working with other levels of government, rather than dictate to them in their own areas of jurisdiction. I can say quite bluntly that when I had my first meeting with social affairs Ministers of the provinces almost four years ago, they clearly stated to me that they felt the federal Government had no role in child care, that it was solely within provincial jurisdiction.
August 11, 1988

I think it is important for the House and the country to understand the jurisdictional arguments in any social policy development. While I know that Members opposite in their political rhetoric or editorial writers might feel that those are not major considerations, some of us have had enough experience in social policy to know that if we cannot consult and do not work with the provinces on social policy those policies are doomed to failure.
I remind Members as they begin debate not to forget the history of social policy programs. If they were to be effective, they had to be flexible and involve provincial co-operation. I do not say 100 per cent unanimity or consensus, but we need to have provincial co-operation. If people do not believe in flexibility, may I remind my colleagues opposite of 1966. Pensions come under provincial jurisdiction. Canadians wanted a national pension plan. Today we call it the Canada Pension Plan. In Quebec we call it the Quebec Pension Plan. Even at that time we got a national plan with a distinct component for Quebec. It was said at that time that we needed a national plan but that to get it we had to have flexibility. We had to understand the regions. We had to be respectful of that. If that was valid in 1966, and today the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan have become a major component in pension and retirement planning, then is it not surely valid today, in 1988?
The other point I make to Members opposite, and regrettably I have had too much experience in opposition-
And you are going to get some more.

speechtext:
Annualized. That is the program they have in mind. I say to them that they can criticize, but what they should not be quite so sensitive about is our looking at their proposals, analysing them, and criticizing them. They also must meet certain criteria. Are they acceptable to Canadians? Are they affordable?
This program follows a long-standing tradition with respect to cost-sharing arrangements between the federal and provincial levels of government in addressing social problems, that is, a 50-50 balance in sharing the financial load. At the present time, the provinces are receiving, on average, about 35 per cent from the federal Government. Our strategy calls for a doubling of spaces, that is, 200,000 new and subsidized spaces over the next seven years. The federal Government is committed to providing 75 per cent of provincial capital contributions to develop these new spaces in non-profit facilities, as well as 50 per cent operating subsidies for both existing and new nonprofit and commercial spaces.
I say to members of the Opposition that they are opposed to this legislation and they want to delay it as we saw yesterday in the House. They will have to go back to the people, and we will have to let the people decide why they do not have spaces and why the money is not flowing. It is because the NDP and Liberals decided not to approve the legislation.
The "not for profit" spaces which provinces create during this seven-year "boost" period will be eligible for the 75 per cent capital financing. This will substantially reduce the burden on provincial treasuries and help to make our goal a reality. The legislation will also expand eligibility for matching operating funds to both the "not for profit" and commercial sectors, in recognition of the fact that about 40 per cent of the existing number of spaces are in the commercial sector. We would have a great deal of trouble meeting our twin goals of improved quality and availability if we were to ignore almost half the existing system and in some provinces, such as Newfoundland, because of financial considerations, 90 per cent of the system.
Our national strategy and this legislation also recognize that all provinces are not at the same stage in developing their child care services. Some are behind others. That is why the Government has built into the Bill a provision to increase funding for certain provinces based upon the national average entitlement per child. We believe that child care services should be more equally available across the country because Canadian families are facing similar needs no matter where they live. I suggest that if Liberal Members want to criticize that part of the Bill, they should take a look at their own experience in the fifties and sixties and how the medicare formula was used at that time.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
I said earlier that both quality and availability are objectives of our national strategy on child care. It is insufficient simply to create new spaces. Those spaces must provide the kind of quality care that parents demand for their children. At the same time, improving the quality of existing spaces without increasing the number of spaces fails to meet the increasing demands of the services.
That is one reason for the increase of $1 billion in our allocation to the federal-provincial program which I announced a few weeks ago. It is also the reason this Act requires that provincial and territorial governments specify child care service standards as part of the agreements between the two levels of government. It is that method by which we can address the standards issue. Provinces will also be required to establish methods to enforce those standards and to ensure that both the standards and enforcement procedures are widely publicized within each province.
The areas in which standards are to be developed are those areas that contribute the most to improving the quality of child care services. These will include child-staff ratios, group sizes, staff qualifications, program content, parental involvement and, of course, health and safety measures.
I am sure that parents, care givers, and professional groups will be working closely with provincial authorities in developing these standards where they do not now exist. The agreements that we will be negotiating with individual provinces will also include a time period within which these standards are to be put in place.
Under this legislation we are giving provinces the option of negotiating agreements consistent with the national child care strategy or remaining within the day care provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan.
I believe the approach we are taking has significantly higher benefits for provinces than the Canada Assistance Plan program. If we examine the recent history of provincial day care expenditures and reimbursements under CAP, it is clear that we are proposing a significant increase in our commitment to child care services across the country. Over the last few years the federal Government, through CAP, shared about 30 per cent of provincial expenditures on day care. As I have mentioned, that figure will be substantially higher under the Canada Child Care Act.
In addition, I remind Members that in the four years the Government has been in office, even under the Canada Assistance Plan we have increased by 100 per cent the amount of money the Canada Assistance Plan has made available to the provinces and child care givers for child care.
When I hear Liberals saying "you haven't done enough" or "you haven't done anything", in relation to what they were doing that is a rather interesting wicket on which to try to build a case.
Under the terms of the new Canada Child Care Act, the federal Government alone will be committing some $4 billion to child care services, or twice the total combined federal and provincial expenditures of the last six years. The federal proportion of expenditures will increase on average to about 50 per cent and could, in some instances in some provinces, be as high as 90 per cent given the funding formula and the top up provisions for certain provinces.
I think those few statistics demonstrate how much better off provinces will be under the Canada Child Care Act and how much more they will be able to do with the stronger financial support being provided by the Government. The point of our strategy is not to reduce what provinces have been doing but to provide the financial incentive for them to be doing more. Our commitment reflects what provinces can realistically achieve over the next seven years.
All agreements signed with provinces prior to April 1, 1990 will be retroactive to April 1, 1988. For the benefit of our viewers, April 1, 1988, is the beginning of this fiscal year. We have said right along that the money would flow in this fiscal year, and the money will flow as of April 1, 1988. All we now need for the money to be available to the provinces is the passage of this Bill in order that we can sign the federal-provincial agreements. This means that the provinces need not fear that their current activities toward expanding child care services will not be covered, despite the fact that this legislation is being given second reading today and needs passage.
I know that some Members opposite hold some strong views on the issue of child care services. I am sure that all Members agree, however, on the need to improve the availability, quality, acceptability, and afffordability of child care services as a necessity for working parents and for healthy, happy families and children.
On this side of the House we have concluded that our national strategy on child care best meets this need in a manner that respects the rights and obligations of parents, addresses the concerns of provincial authorities, and adapts flexibility to differing regions and community values. As I said when I began my remarks, determining the proper balance and flexibility in social policy initiatives is an important although difficult undertaking. In the final analysis, setting realistic objectives and developing a workable means to achieve those objectives is the only way to achieve progress.
I truly believe that this policy represents a substantial step forward in meeting the needs of Canadian families and children. I am looking forward to the passage of this legislation so that we can finalize the arrangements with our provincial counterparts and realize the goals that we have established together. I look forward not only to the debate but to the passage of this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in this House to reply to the Government on Bill C-144, the Canada Child Care Act.
Mr. Speaker, when I read this Bill, I ask myself, while noting that it is a start, where our priorities as a society are and where the priorities of the Mulroney Government are, in view of the fact that a child care system is not a luxury but an urgent necessity.
Our society has changed radically over the past 20 years. Today, less than one Canadian family in six takes the traditional form of the mother working at home and taking care of the childen while the father works outside the home. Moreover, in many families there is only one parent-in most cases a woman raising her children alone. More than half of Canadian women who have pre-school children work outside the home, and in 45 per cent of families with children, both parents have to work outside the home.
However, only 20 per cent of the children have the benefit of licensed day care services. We also know that 57 per cent of children between the ages of 6 and 14 are left alone after school.
Some people say day care is the woman's business. That is false and completely unfair, Mr. Speaker! Day care services are for the couple to choose, for society to choose, and they are a priority the Mulroney Government has already taken too long to get around to.
It is with great regret that I rise today to discuss the Government's feeble child care legislation. The need for an increase in adequate child care spaces in Canada has been fully explained and documented since the first royal commission on the status of women in 1970. The need for child care is widespread.
[ Translation]
Let us recall Katie Cook's task force on child care, which revealed that back in 1985 there were no day care spaces for over 1 million children between the ages of 0 and 12 whose parents worked more than 20 hours a week.

We deem this to be the core need group. It is not surprising, then, that this need has inspired a consensus among Canadians, a consensus to the effect that the time has come for the Canadian Government to implement a cost-sharing program which will meet the needs of Canadian families.
There are three essential problems with the Canada Child Care Act. First, it is not part of a comprehensive program as far as we can see, as no mention is made of other related legislation, notably full employment, parental leave, fiscal
Canada Child Care Act
reform, beyond certain inadequate tax credits mentioned in the White Paper.

Second, this Bill in no way meets the needs of the Canadian family. The mere fact that the target or goal of this Bill is to create only 200,000 spaces over a period of seven years is arguable and unacceptable, since one million children currently lack day care spaces. And when we realize that the special needs of low-income families and latchkey children are completely ignored in this bill, we are faced with a very serious problem, Mr. Speaker.

Third, as we have seen over and over again, there is no mention of standards, or even objectives if the Minister prefers that term, criteria supported by the report on the task force on child care, the report of the Senate subcommittee on child care, and virtually every child care advocacy group that has been consulted.
Before I continue, I want to discuss the idea of choice. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has chosen to present himself as the sole advocate of choice for Canadian families. Let me go on record now in saying that the only way to provide choices for Canadian parents is to provide the necessary funds through a cost-sharing agreement which ensures universal access to child care.
If the Government fails to take this next step, it is denying a number of parents the right to participate in the workforce as well as failing to provide the necessary assistance to single parents and parents of low income families to meet the needs of day-to-day living in a Canadian society. In so doing it will be denying choice, the choice to work in many instances. It will also be preventing Canadians from providing the best possible future for their children.

Living as we are in a time when the birth rate is very low, when poverty afflicts women most, we must face the fact that in Canada today, one child in five is living in poverty and one child in every three is sexually assaulted.
The Government has a responsability to Canadian families, a responsability to our children, and that responsability must be discharged by creating day care spaces and a good child care system. Yet the Mulroney Government says nothing about low-and middle-income families in this bill, and the witnesses who appeared before the child care sub-committees were particularly concerned about this aspect of the new program. They were afraid that the ceiling mentioned in the new program would force the provinces to cut the funding used to subsidize child care for low-income families. We would aim to have parent fees reduced to 50 per cent of the total costs by the early 1990s, with a longer term goal of eventually reducing costs even further. We would provide up to 80 per cent of all government funding for poorer provinces and territories with underdeveloped services. We would insist on parental and community involvement in the development of child care in Canada. This is only common in non-profit centres. We would improve care giver training and wages.
Most important, and I am glad the Minister is here, we would amend the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act to give all parents a real opportunity to spend some time at home with their infant children. The Minister has not mentioned this very important aspect which our committee also recommended.
Working Canadian women and their families have great needs for reliable quality child care services. They had hoped for a national child care program which would be a model social program and which would develop progressively into the future. This is the first social program we have had since medicare. We should have built it on the lines of medicare with national standards, with equal access, and with quality services across the country. Taxpayers want their child care dollars to be well spent.
The Government is generous in the amount of money that is going in at the first stage. I must admit that our plan had even less money targeted during the first stage. We want the money to go directly into child care services so that parents will have a choice and will be assured that they do not have to use an unreliable babysitter or in fact provide no care but can go to
their neighbourhood child care centre or have other forms of family support and in-home services available to them.
This child care legislation is the final straw in a flawed and regressive Conservative child care strategy. It does not even attempt to deal realistically with child care needs of Canada. The Minister has made no attempt to assess the real child care needs. He has taken an arbitrary 200,000 spaces over seven years, laid it on, and, boom, there is nothing after that.
We cannot support this program. We ask the Government, in all sincerity, to withdraw the Bill. Children and women deserve better.

Mr. Speaker, 13 years ago, on August 1, 1975, Canada, along with 33 other nations, including the United States and the Soviet Union, signed a landmark agreement which came to be known as the Helsinki Accords. Canada, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), has given leadership and direction to honour this country's commitment to human rights.
What about elsewhere? Even since glasnost and demok-ratizatsia, some 300 political prisoners, including 10 Helsinki monitors, still languish in labour camps and exile. The recent decision of Romania to bulldoze 7,000 villages, uprooting and scattering the 2.5 million native Hungarians throughout Romania, is a direct affront to those Accords.
Romania undertook to succour all persons under its jurisdiction without distinction of race, sex, language or religion, just as we did. I would urge the Department of External Affairs to show Canada's displeasure at this ruthless uprooting of defenceless minority groups in Romania today.

speakerposition: subtopic

subsubtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND AND LABRADOR-CALL FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the native people of Newfoundland and Labrador have been the victims of an apparently intentional effort by the Government of Canada to deny them the full rights to which they are entitled under Section 91(24) of the Canadian Constitution and the provisions of the Indian Act. Studies commissioned by me, including an examination of official documents, have revealed that from early after Newfoundland joined Confederation in 1949, a systematic denial of rights has been a fact of our history and continues to affect the lives of native people in Newfoundland and Labrador. It amounts to discrimination against native people because they live in this province. It is time for this hidden history to be fully exposed.
I have therefore called upon the Government of Canada to establish immediately a Royal Commission on Native People
in Newfoundland and Labrador. Such a commission would have a mandate to inquire into the treatment of aboriginal peoples since 1949, with specific focus on the rejection by the federal Government of its constitutional responsibilities with respect to the native people in the province. The commission should have the authority to recommend measures to correct the historic and current injustices, and to ensure cultural survival and promote self-government for the native people of Newfoundland and Labrador. This record of official injustice must be exposed and redressed.

Mr. Speaker, today Quebecers are in mourning. Felix Leclerc is being taken to his final rest. A giant is being put to sleep. Felix Leclerc is one of our Quebecois and Canadian poets and singers who set the tone for us, who gave us a taste for Quebec, especially in his songs and poems. August 11, 1988

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-ACTION TAKEN BY UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians across this great country can rejoice at our latest victory in the fight against acid rain. This Government has been pursuing quiet diplomacy. Perhaps it is not the confrontation method the Opposition would have preferred, but we have succeeded.
Last Friday, President Reagan announced that his administration would freeze U.S. emissions of nitrogen oxides at 1987 levels for seven years. Finally, all the hard work of this Government and the Acid Rain Committee is paying off.
No one in Canada doubts that acid rain is a killer and that a great deal of work needs to be done. This summer the information campaign engineered by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has proven to be highly successful in making the average American aware of our concerns and the damage this problem is creating for both our countries.
This is only the beginning, and every day we are making progress. The Americans realize more and more how critical this problem is and that we must combine our efforts to combat this menace called acid rain. Let us give credit where credit is due and encourage our Minister of the Environment to continue his good work.

speechtext: 1985 GANDER AIR CRASH-CALL FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY

Mr. Speaker, the investigation into the 1985 Gander Arrow air crash has been plagued with controversy, contradiction, resignations and confusion. Crucial testimony has been neglected, documents have been hidden from the Canadian Aviation Safety Board members, and tentative conclusions have been nothing short of illogical.
Now there are new revelations. Several firemen who worked on extinguishing the fire resulting from this unfortunate crash are ill from what they believe to be the ingestion of toxic gases. What caused those toxic fumes? What caused fire extinguishing equipment to activate prior to the plane crashing? Why is information being withheld from the Canadian Aviation Safety Board? We need a public commission of inquiry into the Gander air crash. We must find out the truth about this most unfortunate disaster.

August 11, 1988

subsubtopic: FEDERAL MEASURES TO ASSIST WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Government has made three particularly significant contributions toward the economic health of Canada's West.
First was the Western Accord which started the process, now completed, of dismantling the punitive National Energy Program.
Second was the Western Economic Diversification Program which, in its first year, approved 231 proposals for $44 million in assistance to Alberta businesses as of the end of July. There were 503 proposals in the whole of western Canada for a total investment of $345 million. Twelve Calgary companies received assistance ranging from $20,000 to $720,000. Not only does this assist in broadening our economic base, it also creates jobs.
Last month we had the announcement of the western procurement initiative which will increase the amount of federal procurement carried out in western Canada by more than $600 million over the next four years. That is an increase of 16 per cent. In addition, our Government is committed to sourcing a greater portion of contracts over $100 million from western suppliers.
Who can say that this Government has not responded to the needs of western Canada? No one!

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow at the UN, the Special Committee on Decolonization will consider the illegal occupation of East Timor since 1975 by Indonesia. Since that time Indonesia has waged a genocidal war against the people of East Timor.

committee unanimously reported to the House a recommendation that with the omnibus Trade Bill in the United States not giving an exemption to Canada we should not proceed with the trade agreement. At the same time, Ambassador Gotlieb, on behalf of the Government of Canada, wrote to the United States administration and Congressional leaders that: "The proposed redefinition of subsidy represents a significant and dangerous departure from generally accepted international norms. If enacted, they would undermine the GATT".
On Section 103 of that same Bill, Ambassador Gotlieb said: "These proposals could lead to U.S. actions inconsistent with the GATT and would exacerbate international trade tensions".
Yesterday the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade said the Government of Canada no longer has a problem with that Bill. He said that all of the matters have been dealt with and that there is no problem. Yet the very same concerns and issues raised by Ambassador Gotlieb are still in the Bill.
Is the Parliamentary Secretary speaking for the Government? If so, why has the Government changed its position? Why is the Government abandoning its previous position stated by the full Commons committee? Why is the Government not protesting U.S. trade action that will continue to harass Canadian exporters?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question by my hon. friend is whether the Parliamentary Secretary, in his response, spoke for the Government. May I say that not only has the Parliamentary Secretary spoken for the Government, he has done so in an eloquent, effective, and tremendous way here in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: We are talking about McDermid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: The House Leader of the New Democratic Party insists on naming him. Yes, it was McDermid who did such a wonderful job.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if it is true that the Parliamentary Secretary in his own fashion is speaking for the Government, then the question stands. Why is the Government retreating from its position? Why has it changed the stated position of the Minister in the House that we would protest those measures in the omnibus Trade Bill which contravene the trade agreement even though those measures are still in the Bill as it has been passed by the Congress? Why has the Government once again lost its backbone when it comes to protecting Canadian interests and has subjected Canadian exporters to further trade harassment?
August 11, 1988

Why are we perpetrating a joke on the Canadian people by having tougher trade laws?

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:

He has done a masterful job of representing our interests in Washington and should be recognized.
Second, we have reviewed the text of the omnibus Trade Bill and we are satisfied there are no provisions in it that would require the administration to take any action which would be inconsistent with the free trade agreement. We have examined that. We have not retreated one iota on this. The free trade agreement is going ahead. We look forward to debating the silly amendments the Hon. Member has brought into the House.

speechtext:

The Prime Minister knows that the American President has signed a Bill authorizing compensation to individual Japanese-American survivors. Recognizing that the issue of individual compensation has been the sticking point in all the discussions with the National Association of Japanese Canadians, will the Prime Minister now authorize negotiations with the National Association of Japanese Canadians on the issue of individual compensation for Japanese-Canadian survivors?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-ISSUE OF INDIVIDUAL COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am happy, Mr. Speaker, to refer again to the support of the New Democratic Party for the position I raised in the House of Commons in June of 1984. My hon. friend refers to the fact that compensation was the "sticking point". Compensation was not the sticking point. The sticking point was the refusal of the Liberal Government for 40 years to even acknowledge and apologize for what had taken place.

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-ISSUE OF INDIVIDUAL COMPENSATION
speechtext: What about right now?

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-ISSUE OF INDIVIDUAL COMPENSATION

Since this Government has been sworn in, and with the support of my hon. friend in the New Democratic Party, certainly not elsewhere, there has been arranged an

agreement whereby there is to be a trust fund with respect to anti-racism. There is to be a formal apology delivered in the House of Commons on behalf of the Government and the people of Canada with respect to this tragedy that took place so many years ago.

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-ISSUE OF INDIVIDUAL COMPENSATION
speechtext: But no negotiations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-ISSUE OF INDIVIDUAL COMPENSATION

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that the Prime Minister's word "negotiate" describe a reality that has not been followed since January of 1985. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister to give his word on behalf of this Government that there will be full and fair discussions with the National Association of Japanese Canadians to arrive at an agreement acceptable to the association to provide the kind of redress that is essential if this blot on the national honour is finally to be expunged.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for referring to this matter because it is indeed a very serious blot on Canada's honour and, to me, it is a matter of very considerable regret that for over 40 years this matter was left untouched by the previous series of administrations. We have made some important progress with respect to resolving the matter and, with the support of my hon. friend, hopefully this matter can be brought to a proper and appropriate resolution which will be satisfactory to all concerned.

subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF SOUTH AFRICAN IMMIGRANTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Employment and Immigration my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It concerns the Government's soft policy on South Africa. There are in Canada a number of white South Africans here as draft resisters, unwilling on conscientious grounds to serve in the Armed Forces to enforce apartheid, who face possible imprisonment if they return home. They are uncertain as to whether they will be allowed to remain in Canada. There are non-white South Africans here in Canada because they oppose living in a racist society and fascist country, who are also uncertain about their future in Canada.
Will the Prime Minister today declare that South Africans will have blanket approval to obtain landed immigrant status in Canada provided they are admissible under the Immigration Act, as did the former Government with its B-I list, including such countries as El Salvador and Lebanon, countries in Eastern Europe and other countries as well?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF SOUTH AFRICAN IMMIGRANTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will, of course, as a Government, look with care at any question that is raised with respect to Canada and Canada's role, and the succour Canada can provide to refugees or people seeking our assistance. We have done that before and we will do so again in this case.
My friend will understand that I must take exception to his reference to a "soft policy" of this Government on South Africa. The former Ambassador to the United Nations, Stephen Lewis, referred to the tremendous leadership shown by Canada in the United Nations with respect to South Africa. The comments of my hon. friend have been repudiated by President Mugabe, President Kaunda, and Prime Minister Ghandi, all of whom believe that Canada since 1984 has been playing a particular and effective role of international leadership with respect to South Africa.

speechtext:

Africans seeking haven here, and so a signal will be sent to South Africans in their own country who want to resist the official policy of apartheid in that country?

I think it is quite clear that this Government has made its position known on South Africa very forcefully. We have assumed a position of leadership as was demonstrated recently in the sports community. We are very conscious of the role we want to play in the world in this respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of State for Finance. The Minister is, of course, aware of the hearings which the Finance Committee held on bank charges. He is also aware of the representations the small business community across Canada has been making to him and to Members of Parliament that many of the same recommendations, made concerning bank service charges to the consumer, by the Finance Committee, be applied to small business. Many small businesses feel captured by the banks and feel that they are unable to object to many unfair charges imposed by the banks.
Is the Minister prepared to act on behalf of the small business community of Canada against the big banks?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: SERVICE CHARGES APPLIED TO SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the Government is prepared to act. We made this clear a good number of months ago.
First, all the principles which we came up for the consumer: disclosure, advance notice, a complaints mechanism, and abolishment of obnoxious charges, should be applied to the business community as well.
The Hon. Member is very late in coming to this issue. We have a meeting today between the small business organizations and the Bankers' Association. I hope they will be able to resolve the details to make sure that we can have in place a regime just as strong for the small business sector as we have for consumers.

speechtext:
I rise in deference to the Chair but not in deference to common sense. I did not mean to stimulate a national debate yesterday. I really thought we were going to go on to serious things yesterday. In view of the ungainly, unseemly conduct of the New Democrats on something so fundamental as child care, I suggest today, because of the way the New Democrats treated child care yesterday, that my question of privilege on dress for Members is most relevant indeed. If the legislators of the land cannot be dressed comfortably in the halls that make laws, what hope do we have for child care, Mr. Speaker?
Having said that, I am not trying to impede the progress of the House. I sit on the far right wing of the front bench of the Tory Party, and I am glad to be a member of the Tory Party and/or sit on the right wing. Having raised the question of dress I would like to show to my colleagues and to you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not necessarily right wing totally in most situations. If we are inane and stupid enough to meet here on August 10 in the middle of the summer, then I suggest it is time we got our dress code to conform to the realities of the land.

To quote your words, you would not recognize me "because he was not dressed according to the customs and traditions of the House and, until he is, he will not be recognized". This was your reply to my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), whose area raises second grade apples.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

I know that Hon. Members would want me to thank the Hon. Member from Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) for his impetuous and interesting intervention.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before I recognize the Hon. Minister, earlier today during the course of debate on second reading of Bill C-144, the Hon. Member for Outremont proposed to move the following reasoned amendment on which the Chair reserved:
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the word "That" and by substituting the following:
"This House objects to the principle of Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, which is to establish a program that does not provide access and services in all provinces and equal access to low and middle income families."
After consideration, the Chair finds a major procedural difficulty with the wording of the proposed amendment. As stated in Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 744(1), a reasoned amendment "must be declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the Bill". In her amendment the Hon. Member simply indicates her objection to the principle of the Bill and, as indicated in Beauchesne's Citation 745(4), "an amendment which amounts to no more than a direct negation of the principle of the Bill is open to objection".
August 11, 1988

I must therefore rule the amendment out of order as it does not constitute a reasoned amendment and as it amounts, in its form, to an expanded negative.
May I point out to the Hon. Member and the House that the results sought by the amendment can be achieved by simply voting against the principle of the Bill, that is, by voting against the second reading motion. Furthermore, the Chair would like to remind the House that the text of a reasoned amendment should include words indicating that the House does not wish to give a Bill second reading. For that purpose, I refer Hon. Members to page 531 of Erskine May's Twentieth Edition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to address Bill C-144, the Canada Child Care Act. As my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), indicated, this Bill provides for implementation of the most important component of the national strategy on child care. It responds to the child care needs of Canadians with an innovative, flexible policy that is both generous and equitable. It represents a major move forward for children, parents, and families throughout the country.
Child care is probably one of the most pressing social issues facing legislators today. This Bill reflects this Government's strong commitment to improve the quality and quantity of care in all regions of the country. The Government will spend $6.4 billion on child care over the next seven years, and another $1 billion annually after that. This is a significant response to the realities of our society today and lays the foundation for an improved quality of life for the Canadian family in the future.
As Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, I am especially pleased that the national strategy on child care has been expanded to recognize the special needs and concerns of Indian people. Indians must be full and productive participants in society if Canada is to go into the 21st century a more mature and stronger nation. Today a wide range of federal programs and services is provided to Indians. For example, CMHC has a rural and native housing program, DRIE's native economic development program, and CEIC's native internship program.
Mr. Speaker, Indians must also have access to child care, child care that is both flexible and affordable, so that they can concentrate on their jobs and improve their quality of life. As Hon. Members are aware, despite progress made in recent years, economic conditions in Indian communities lag behind the national average. This means that the ability of an Indian family to find good child care for its children while one or both parents work can be essential to that family's well being.
I am very glad to say that as a result of this Government's initiative, some 2,000 child care spaces for Indian children will
Canada Child Care Act
be created over six years, that is, for children living on reserves.
However, creating child care spaces according to the provincial model will not resolve a specifically Indian problem. Like all Canadians, Indians are very concerned about their children's well being, and anyone who visits Indian families living on reserves will see how important children are to those families. Child care must therefore meet safety and other standards while also respecting the social and cultural traditions of the group in question, in this case the Indians.
Mr. Speaker, Indian child care in Canada is underdeveloped. Most provincial governments have been reluctant to extend their programs to Indian reserves since they are, admittedly, a federal responsibility.
Only the Province of Ontario finances Indian child care through a contribution agreement with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. On some reserves, bands have set up their own daycare, but such cases are few and far between.

The Government of Canada has a special relationship with Indian people living on reserves. It was in recognition of this relationship that Health and Welfare Canada, in consultation with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, developed the special Indian component of the national strategy on child care. This component provides for an expenditure of $60 million over six years to develop and stimulate the growth of accredited child care services on reserves. This is the first time in Canada's history that such funds have been made available specifically to serve the needs of Indian children.
Although the administrative details of this initiative are yet to be worked out, the funding schedule has been set and some basic goals and principles have been established for the program. Beginning April 1, 1989, the Government of Canada will invest $5 million in each of the first two years of the program, $10 million in each of the third and fourth years, and $15 million in each of the final two years of the program. The funds will be administered by Health and Welfare Canada with assistance from Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
This money will be used to fund a number of significant pilot projects designed to determine exactly what is needed in terms of Indian child care and how to deliver that. It is anticipated that the program will create about 2,000 child care spaces over six years. Equally as important, it will help us establish how the Indian child care system should work.

Mr. Speaker, obviously Indians will be fully consulted on the implementation of this program in their communities, as will the provinces. Since this Government came to power, we have always taken this approach, and we intend to start consultations in the very near future.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Mr. Speaker, we have reason to expect that the program will develop in such a way that Indians will be able to exercise direct control over a child care system that is also in line with our approach to the provision of services to Indians.
Our primary objective will be to create services, with and for Indians, which respect Indians values, traditions and culture. Indian child care should not merely reflect the kind of system established by the provinces. It will be thoroughly Indian, while meeting current standards for health, safety, child-staff ratios, staff accreditation and licensing.

I want to emphasize that Indians will continue to have access to the $100 million child care initiative fund, another important element of the Government's national strategy on child care. Among other things, the child care initiative fund supports applied research and demonstration projects which address the needs of certain groups in society. Indians have been designated as one of the target groups for this research and plans are already under way for a major study of child care on Indian reserves.
The fund will help child care training institutions develop course materials which are sensitive to Indian culture and Indians will be encouraged to participate in this special training.
The national strategy on child care is more wide ranging and flexible than any such program ever offered by a federal Government. Today's generation of Indian children must become full and productive partners in the Canada of tomorrow. I am sure that Hon. Members of this House can contribute meaningfully to that future by giving this legislation unqualified support and speedy passage.

Mr. Speaker, for us in the Official Opposition the idea of child care is obviously important. It is an idea whose time has certainly come. How can the Minister possibly consider that his Government has responded to the promise it made in the last election campaign with this program which was not introduced in the four years of its normal mandate and will only create 200,000 additional day care spaces in the coming four-year period when the need, which is recognized by the Government I believe, is for one million additional child care spaces? With the good times which Canada has known in the last four years and the problem which the Government has recognized, how can it say that 200,000 additional spaces to be created over the next four years is an adequate response?

speechtext: Questions and comments are concluded. Debate. The Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan).

Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed being able to participate briefly in the question and comment session with the Hon. Minister about this child care program. When he was pressed on the question of whether he considered the program the Government is delivering today to be adequate fulfilment of the Government's promise to Canadians during the last election, he said "yes". This program will create 200,000 additional day care spaces in the Canadian stock of all day care spaces, including private and public, over a seven-year period.
During the last election campaign, Canadians, particularly the millions of women in the Canadian population, were promised an adequate, comprehensive day care program.
In my riding alone, the day care shortfall today is 20,000 spaces. That means that one-tenth of this magnificent program delivered by the Government to the millions of women to whom it promised adequate child care is needed in one small corner of Metropolitan Toronto. This is not an adequate program.
It is very significant that the program is being delivered today. It is very significant that at the beginning of this debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of Canada stood outside in the hall telling the media that the Government had fulfilled its promise to the women of Canada in delivering this child care program. I think the Government saying that our

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
determination to debate this Bill until the end of today constituted a filibuster is also significant. Why is it a filibuster? This is the first day the subject has been debated in this House of Commons. It is a one-day debate about a $6 billion program that the Government claims delivers on one of its major promises. We have been brought back in the middle of the summer with an election call, we hope, coming very soon. This Bill has been put on the menu and we are told we have to finish the debate on second reading by the end of the day or we will be accused of filibustering.
Filibustering after two hours.

We will be accused of filibustering after only two hours as my friend from Vancouver observes. I think that is easy to understand. The Government does not want this matter to be fully debated. It does not want the Canadian people to see what I call the thin suit of its day care program in the light of parliamentary debate and examination. The Government wants a one-liner. It wants to be able to say it delivered on a promise to establish a comprehensive day care program in Canada, and the less said about it, the better, because when we look at this program we find it is a pathetic farce and fraud. It is a particular fraud on the women of Canada. They are the ones for whom this program is the most meaningful.
Members opposite like to blame all their shortcomings on the former Government. I was a Minister in the former government and I was proud of it. However, we were not a government that was in a position to deliver the programs required by this country for all time. The need for day care is something that snuck up on the people of Canada and on successive governments. We were not as sensitive as we should have been in the past, and I mean all of us, to the situation of women. We did not recognize until very recently that what we thought was the typical family was very far from the typical family. A typical family, we thought, was one where one of the spouses, the wife, in most cases, was at home looking after the children. If she was not, she was out working to provide fulfilling activity for herself, to enrich her life and to provide some extra spending money to supplement the earnings of the main bread-winner, the husband. But anyone who thinks that is the typical family today has a lot to learn and one can learn it in my riding and in any other riding in our country.
The fact is that there are very few families where there is a spouse living at home and keeping the home fires going as the main occupation. Women are working and in a lot of cases they are the only wage earner in the family. They are the bread-winner. They are working to support their families and we are tying a hand behind their backs by not having an adequate day care program.
Until medicare was established, we caused suffering in Canada by not having such a program. Medicare is now a program equally meaningful to men and women. Day care is not. I think we should be blunt about recognizing that part of the reason for the delay in bringing in day care was the fact that this place was mainly peopled by men with the perspective that did not recognize the actual facts of family life and the terrible burden carried by women in our society. I see this, if
not during the rest of the year, in election campaigns, when I make a point of being at bus-stops and subway stations at six-thirty in the morning when people in my riding are going to work on a typical day. I see the women, not the men, leading young children to whatever kind of day care arrangements they have been able to make so they can go out and make a living in order to keep their families going.
The Minister has the nerve to say that Canada cannot afford a better day care program than a measly 200,000 additional spaces to be created over the next five years. That man should be ashamed of himself when he makes such a statement like that about the economic and social needs of our society and about the simple question of social justice in the field of day care. To wait until a hot summer day, probably hours before an election will be called, to try to twist our arms so that we do not have time to tell the Canadian people the truth about this fraudulent effort to validate a campaign promise is too much. I do not think we should let the Bill go through today even though it is an important measure and even though I would rather have 200,000 additional day care spaces than none.
We cannot let this Bill go through without letting the Canadian people hear what is wrong with it. In the last election campaign, three big beautiful promises were made to the Canadian people about day care by each of the national Parties. The Liberals made their promise as well as the New Democratic Party and the Conservatives. Each was different. I was interested in the subject, and I am glad to be able to speak today, because it is the most important issue in my riding, in my opinion.
The issue of day care can bring out on a day's notice a large crowd of people, mainly women, with babies in their arms, with problems they are looking at the legislators of this country to solve. We have seen this in the front pages of the newspapers in Toronto over the last few days as a municipal government tries to cope with the delivery of a social service without adequate help, without comprehensive help, from the federal Government. Yet the municipal government, which mainly draws its revenue from property taxes is continuing to provide the level of service it did in the past, although a low level, at great difficulty to its own tax base.
I am not saying it is easy to finance a day care program for Canada, but it is important. It is essential and the sensible economic development of our country requires that we do it.
The promises of each of the political Parties were different and only one of those Parties won the last election. The Conservatives won with 211 Members of Parliament. That promise was what meant the most in my riding. I think people were expecting that when the Conservatives were elected they would deliver a universal, comprehensive day care program that would solve the problem the way the old age pension has solved the problem of our senior citizens being the poorest Canadians in our society-they were before but they are no longer-and the way in which medicare solved the problem of poor people and people in poor regions not being able to afford proper medical care. Medicare solved that problem. People expected that a strong Conservative Government with a sacred trust to keep would have delivered that program.
August 11, 1988

Our program, which I hope I will have time to talk about in a moment, was not brought forward because we were not the government. The NDP program, which I do not agree with, but which would have done a lot more than the program delivered by the Government, is on the shelf because the NDP did not form the Government either. The Government frittered away its majority and its claim on five years or four years of control of the House to deliver a comprehensive day care program. In the dying hours of Parliament we have a pathetic attempt by the Government to make the women and the people of the country think that it is fulfilling a campaign promise that we expected would be fulfilled five years since.

I wish to pay tribute to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin), our child care critic who has worked very hard for the past four years, on all the reviews requested by the Government, all the committees that drafted their reports and were directed by the Government to proceed with a review of the work they had already done. The Hon. Member finally produced a report which we in the Official Opposition have adopted as our own.

I am proud to have circulated the Official Opposition's proposals on child care. They are comprehensive and they cost a lot more than the ones before us today, but they will work and give us a day care program; not the type of program that the NDP have talked about which is delivered in state-owned institutions to children across the country, and not a program which forces the closure of day care programs run by women in their homes in my riding. As far as we are concerned, for profit types of day care centres are perfectly acceptable. In the Liberal Party we have no objection ideologically to entrepreneurs who believe that they can deliver a good day care program and make money at it. In our view there is absolutely nothing objectionable to that. In fact, we propose to stimulate their activities by providing government funds to them under circumstances that I have described.
Misuse of tax dollars.

The NDP consider that a misuse of funds. I hope that we will be talking about that in the next election campaign. Certainly day care will still be an issue in the next election campaign. Perhaps the Conservatives will have nothing more to say about it except to claim that they did what they promised. In my riding, in Toronto, and in places where people have turned their backs on the Conservatives, they will be wanting to know what type of real, serious, effective day care programs will be introduced after the next election when hopefully a Party other than that presently on your right, Mr. Speaker, will have the opportunity to keep some of its promises on the subject of day care.
I have talked about the inadequacy of the day care program delivered by the Government. One other fundamental difficulty with that program is that it does not establish national standards. The Government revels in the concept of consultation and how wonderful it is to consult with the provinces and
Canada Child Care Act
to consult with the groups in society that are interested in an issue. That is motherhood, and it is easy to agree with. Even the former Government recognized that consultation was desirable. It is not a contradiction of the concept of consultation to also advance the concept of leadership.
Canadians expect the Government to provide leadership, and expect Parliament to provide leadership. They particularly expect it when we are talking about money being spent through the Government that has been raised from the Canadian people. We have taken their money through taxes and we have established a priority. The basic principle of democratic accountability requires us to provide some leadership in the area in which we are turning over that money to be spent, whether by provincial governments, day care agencies, or whatever it is. We must establish some standards. After all, we are using the money received from the voters. We have to be accountable for some type of standard.
This Government does not understand or agree with that fundamental principle. It feels it is enough to say how it feels and then to write cheques across the country and let those who get the money deliver the program or a substitute for the program at whatever level they consider proper. I do not think that Canadians want that type of federal government. In a country with such a diversity as ours in economic standards the Canadian people want Parliament to set objectives or to set standards for the child care program. We want to support a national level in as many areas of Canadian life as possible, and certainly in those areas where we are turning over federal taxpayers' money to keep programs going.
I deplore the feature of this day care program which does not establish any standards. It says to the provinces: "It's your jurisdiction. You may establish programs. Here is some money, we hope that you will spend it wisely". We ought to do better than that, and Canadians expect us to do better than that. Failure to show leadership in this area and in many other areas is a reason why Canadians are turning their backs on the Conservatives and why their standing is as low as it is with the Canadian people.
I want to share with people in the House the dilemma that one has on how to vote on second reading of a measure as bad as this. We support child care. We want to see federal tax dollars and federal standards and objectives established in this area of child care. The Government has brought forward a measure which we feel is a political fraud because it does not deliver an effective universal child care program. Yet the Government will characterize it as such. Therefore, it is a dilemma. We want to indicate to the Canadian people that we support child care. We want to see this $6.4 billion spent in the area of child care. With our recent amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin), which was not found to be in order, we wanted to demonstrate that this program is terribly lacking. I hope that in the speeches that will be delivered by members of the Official Opposition we will be able to indicate that we want the $6.4 billion to be spent over the next seven years. We want more to be spent. We do not approve of a program that is so woefully inadequate and so fraudulent in political terms.
