Mr. Speaker, 1 have a number of questions. I obviously do not have enough time for them, but I would like to, first of all, clarify a couple of points that the Member made. I must say that I am surprised to see this Member, whom I have a great deal of respect for, repeating some of the misinformation that the Minister himself is promoting regarding the NDP policy. First of all, does he not realize that non-profit day care, which is what we advocate, is not the same as government institutions? There could be public day care as well. We have no objection to that. I wish that he would check into that and clarify that non-profit societies are quite a different thing than government institutions. We are saying that we believe that federal money should go to child care that is not for profit. On the other hand, we are not opposed to commercial day care, providing it is self-sustaining. If parents want to use it and pay fees for it, fine. We are not saying that it should not be commercial. We are saying that it should not be supported by tax dollars. I wish he would be more clear about that.
We are also very much in favour of in-home day care. We want women in the home or people in the home to be licensed as family day care homes, so that they will have decent pay in order to have the chance for all the resources and support that they need. They will have money to get fences and everything will be prepared the way it should be. There would be good quality family day care homes, not just baby-sitting with kids plunked in front of a TV set. If parents still want to use casual informal care, that is their right. We should not be paying federal money. I wanted to clarify those points first.
I will now get to my question. The former Minister, who is well informed on matters of justice, mentioned the question of national objectives. I do not agree with what he was saying and what the Liberals keep saying about national standards. It is not the role of the federal Government to establish standards in areas that are provincial jurisdiction. This was analysed over and over again in our committee, with considerable expertise on this.
In both medicare and health and welfare, the question of standards are a provincial jurisdiction, but certainly those standards should be based on principles. I would ask him to clarify a little bit more the significance of not having national objectives. Also, does he feel, as I do, that the Government seems to be trying to push this particular social program-the only new social program that we have had for many, many years-through before Meech Lake is applied, and has deliberately not put in "the national objectives", which would be required under the Meech Lake Accord?
There is no statement of principles on which provinces would be required to base their standards. There is also no enforcement mechanism as we have in medicare. I wonder if he would comment further on that and if he has any suggestions as to how this should be developed in a way that is closer to the medicare model.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member got up and stated the NDP policy in her own way, because she can certainly state it better than I can, and I accept her statement of her own policy. I am glad also that I can emphasize a very important difference that emerges between the NDP and the Liberals on this subject. That is, we do not think that for-profit operations are bad. We think that they may be entitled to receive support from the taxpayers if they are prepared to meet the standard of the programs-
You better read the studies.

The Member is indicating that the studies may show that there is something wrong with some of the profit day care centres, but that may be all the more reason why the federal Government ought to turn to them, or to turn to them through the provinces, and encourage them, with tax dollars, to do something. For the life of me, I do not accept as a principle-and I know that the NDP do-that when something is run for profit it is not going to be run as well as something that is non-profit.
Where does the profit come from?
I think that profit and the opportunity to make profit assures an efficient operation. Now, efficiency-
Read the studies. That is not true.

I did not interrupt the Hon. Member while she was speaking. Efficiency can be a very desirable component of any operation. There is nothing wrong with having an operation more efficient, providing that it is delivering the goods. If day care can be delivered efficiently by entrepreneurs and profit produced at the bottom line, I do not think that we should turn our backs on it. I think in fact it has a lot to commend it. That is the difference between the way that the Liberals look at things and the way that the NDP look at them.
The Hon. Member made a comment about standards. She does not feel-and I am shocked to hear it-that it is the place of the federal Government to set standards. Well, maybe the difference between us is semantic. I do not mean by standard precise definitions, ceiling heights of rooms where day care centres are to be established, or fire regulations or things like that. I recognize that these are matters which are very regionalized across our country. To try to specify construction materials and size and shape, and even hours, can be totally out of whack with local standards in a particular community.
August 11, 1988

But I insist that it should be the part of the federal Government, wanting to provide leadership, and hopefully a government does want to provide leadership, to set as much of a national standard as it can. We have done this to a degree in medicare, a degree that I think we can be quite proud of. We have not only made sure that high quality medicare is available right across our country, in poor parts of our country and in well-off parts of our country, but that it is accessible, wherever it is found, to poor people and to people who are well off. That is the kind of national standard or national objective that I would like to see.
Finally, the Elon. Member wanted me to comment on the Meech Lake idea about opting out, I suppose, of a shared-cost program. I hope that this would be a program where all the provinces would want to participate. The question of opting out and sharing costs and having different programs and getting compensation for them would not arise. That, after all, is a matter for the federal Government to negotiate. If the federal Government goes about it in a sensible way and has the support of the Canadian people, I do not see why provinces would want to opt out and to provide programs of their own that might be different and lead to the test of whether they meet national objectives or not.
In other words, I would like to see programs rather than references to the Supreme Court of Canada about the interpretation of Meech Lake.
Mis. Copps: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member whether, in his assessment of the situation in his own community, the excessive demand in the City of Toronto, for example, where they have more than 1,000 children on a waiting list, trying to get into available spaces, this program will in any way alleviate that incredible demand.

1 am glad that the Hon. Member asked me about Toronto, because she is an expert not only in Toronto but in Hamilton as well. I did my own research on the subject and found that the demand in my riding of York Centre, unfilled, is for 20,000 additional day care spaces. That is just for one riding, one corner, of the municipality of Metropolitan Toronto. Those 20,000 spaces are needed now, not spread out over the next four years.
We have a program that delivers to our whole country
200,000	spaces, and over the next seven years you will see the total inadequacy of it. I do not think that the Government deserves our co-operation in rubber stamping this Bill by ten o'clock tonight so that they can go out to the country and claim that they fulfilled a promise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is apparent the New Democrats do not like to hear the truth.
I would like to go on with something else that was mentioned. Only 11.5 per cent of these children can be assured of quality licensed care. I take a little bit of exception to that because the Member said that other children are in the care of relatives, neighbours, nannies, or baby-sitters and are in unreliable care. I do not believe the care of a grandmother, a neighbour or a nanny is necessarily unreliable care.
I did not say that either.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
I come from a single parent family. When I was seven years old my father died and I was raised by a single parent mother. Fortunately, I had a very loving mother who gave me good care. I know what it is like to be a child of a single parent. I also worked when my two children were born. I had to work throughout their upbringing and used care outside of the home as well as within the home. I was fortunate in that my husband shared that care with me. He looked after the children while I was at work and I looked after them when he was at work. I had the help of family and I also had to use outside care. It was licensed care and it was not non-profit care but it was care given by a very loving woman because she cared for children. Yes, she made a profit but that did not mean the care was any less. So I have been involved in some of what we are talking about today.
I really find it difficult when so much is being said that care cannot be good care unless it is non-profit licensed care. Care, and good care, comes from the people giving that care. It does not matter whether people are getting paid for it through a non-profit system or a profit system, they are doing it out of the love of caring for children. They are doing it as a neighbour for maybe minimal dollars. Nobody looks after children because they want an easy job. Nobody looks after children just to make money. You cannot look after children unless you really care about them. If you care about children you care about the quality of the care given to them.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East went on to say that Tory Members on the child care committee favoured the traditional family. I do not make any apologies for saying that we favoured the traditional family. We recognize that we have traditional families still in this country. Traditional families also have needs as far as raising children are concerned and have to be included in any policy that we set.
Most single parents in this country are in that position by circumstance, not necessarily by choice. They need help in raising children. The legislation before us will continue to give them the help with the care they need. The legislation also recognizes that parents who are at home require help. It also recognizes that where two parents work and are paying for their child care they deserve some recognition for the dollars they pay out. This legislation recognizes the cost of child care and allows parents to make the choice of and how they will
care for their children. It also recognizes that when those children are under school age that cost of care is more expensive. They should, therefore, have a higher tax allowance. We have done that.
The Member went on to say that the Tories on the committee said that quality was not needed. That is not true. We all agreed, unanimously, on the committee that quality was very important. Where we disagreed is how that quality could be delivered. I mentioned earlier that quality is delivered by caring people in the child care field whether or not it is for profit. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East and the Hon. Member for Outremont would have to agree that as we crossed this country and visited 31 cities in every province and the territories, in the small towns and large towns, we listened to what the people of Canada wanted as far as the care of their children was concerned. Quality was definitely one of the items they were looking for. Quality came in many different ways and certainly was not synonymous with non-profit licensed care.
The Member also mentioned that we took $2.3 billion away from services. We did not take $2.3 billion away from services. We took $2.3 billion and have directed it to parents to allow them to care for their children and meet their responsibilities in raising them. They can decide how they want to raise their children. While we directed to parents $2.3 billion through the tax system, we also invested some $4 billion to provide additional day care spaces. All I have heard so far in this debate is that we are limiting growth to 200,000 spaces. It needs to be said that we are directing subsidized funding to create 200,000 spaces that we will share with the provinces, spaces to help those who cannot pay for their own child care. That is only growth in the subsidized spaces, not in total child care spaces in this country. For those people who can afford child care and can pay for it out of their own pocket, that space is not one of the 200,000.
As the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kilgour) said, he sees nothing wrong with the profit side of the picture coming into child care. If the need is there, entrepreneurs will create the spaces for children and supply those spaces. We heard from some excellent people who had turned their homes into child care centres. Some had 10 or 12 children in them and some had as few as 5. They provided good care. The entrepreneurs are not large chain systems which do not care about children. Entrepreneurs are neighbours, friends and relatives who care about children and are willing to go into the market to provide spaces for children.
Then the Member mentioned that there was no provision for latchkey children. The Hon. Member knows better than that. There is nothing in the legislation that restricts the beginning or the continuance of after-school and pre-school programs. It is part of the over-all child care provisions in the provinces.
August 11, 1988

The Province of Quebec has a system in which the school boards themselves are involved. For other provinces provide the space is provided for child care within the school system but the programs are run by the parents, by non-profit organizations and in some cases by for-profit organizations.
The spaces are there to look after children pre and postschool and they will continue to grow. Under the $100 million initiative fund, which no one on the opposition side has bothered to mention, the total federal dollars that have gone into the care of children, can be used to improve methods for caring for so-called latchkey children. Again, the numbers are inflated in that in many cases, parents may work during school hours but are at home when their children come home from school. We are not dealing with the total number of figures that are being played with in this debate.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East and the Hon. Member for Outremont would also agree that the committee listened to Canadians, not necessarily to people within the House but to Canadians from coast to coast, people who had a very definite interest in coming to the committee to tell us what they felt. Those people said that they do not want the school system to look after latchkey children, they want space within the school. They did not want a curriculum that continues on after three or three-thirty when the children get out of school. They said they wanted space within the schools so that they could run child care programs that meet the needs of the children when they are finished a day in school.
The last thing a child wants when the bell rings at three o'clock is to go into another regimented curriculum after school. They need to let off steam. If they are anything like my boys, they need to let off an awful lot of steam. It is this type of flexibility, recognizing the differences across the country and the need to meet them, that this Bill addresses.
The strategy provides funding for the provinces to deliver child care services under their jurisdictions. We have not intruded upon their jurisdictions whatsoever. As far as standards are concerned, the Hon. Member for Outremont mentioned that there are no standards in place. The Bill provides that the provinces must have standards in place and that they must publicize these standards as well as the methods for their enforcement. There are arrangements to ensure that standards are put into place by the provinces.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East also mentioned that the provinces would be encouraged to use the dollars for poor quality care. I do not believe that the governments of the provinces, no matter what Parties they represent, care so little about children that they would bring in services of poor quality. They too have to answer to the electorate. They have to answer to the parents. More than that, they have to answer to their own consciences. I cannot believe that the Government of any province would be encouraged to use dollars for poor quality service.
Canada Child Care Act
We are working together with the provinces in providing care for the children of Canada. We know from our many tours across Canada and from the people to whom we have listened that people want flexibility. This legislation has addressed the service side of it by putting $4 billion into additional subsidized care spaces for those parents who cannot provide full payment for child care services.
The strategy provides tax measures that allow parents who can pay for child care to realize some return on those dollars that they are putting into the system, providing wages and dollars toward supplies that are required. We have increased the present $2,000 deduction for child care services to $4,000 for pre-schoolers. After that, the tax deduction continues but it remains at $2,000 unless a child is disabled, in which case it remains at $4,000. We have addressed the concerns of parents who are paying for child care services.
Then we come to the parent at home. We could not do as much for the parent at home as we may have liked to do. The parent at home stays at home out of a desire to be in the home with the child. A woman who has a career may come to the point in her life where she must ask what is more important to her as an individual, can she stay home with her child or must she continue to work? That is a very difficult decision for a parent to make, whether it be a father's, a mother's or a joint family decision that is made.
We have tried to recognize the choice these parents make by offering an additional $200 per child that is at home with his or her parent. It may not be enough in some people's eyes. It is certainly not intended as a replacement for wages that might have been earned, but it is a recognition that parents make a conscious decision to stay home and raise children.
In looking back on my life, I worked when my children were young and I only wish that I had been in a position to spend more time with them. I can honestly say that if I had the chance to do it over again, that is probably what I would do. I admire the women who have to make the decision about being in the workforce or staying at home. It is not an easy decision to make, but with this legislation we are attempting to make that decision a little easier to make.
We cannot help all people in all situations, but we can certainly help by working with parents, with care givers and with provincial Governments to ensure that the children of Canada who are our greatest resource receive the care that they truly deserve. I feel that this legislation will do that. It would be nice to be able to do more. There is still more to be done with parental leave which, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver East mentioned, was something that we were unanimous on during the committee hearings. We need to have changes there.
I think we have made headway. We have shown leadership by forming the committee, the first all-parliamentary committee. We listened to 2,000 people across Canada. Because we listened to the people, we have come up with legislation that we feel meets the majority of the needs. Therefore, I move:

Canada Child Care Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the current child care legislation, the Canada Assistance Plan, single parents who are not able to pay for child care are eligible for assistance on a dollar basis and in some cases 100 per cent care. Sometimes it is on a percentage of income basis. To give you an example, we visited a child care centre here in Ottawa which had 44 children in its care. The care of only four of those children was paid for by the parents. The other 40 were subsidized by the Government.
I might mention that as we crossed the country one of the things we heard from parents, advocates, and specialists in the field, was that they wanted to see child care taken out of the Canada Assistance Plan and governed by its own Act. That is exactly what this Government has done. Child care is covered by its own Act so we can be sure the money goes toward child care.
Under this legislation subsidies will still exist. If you have a single parent who cannot afford to pay for the care of her child and she wants to get back into the workforce to improve herself and provide an income to support her children, the
Government can still assist her with the cost of child care through local social service agencies in her community. That has not changed. In fact, it is improved by the fact that not only can the dollars be provided, the federal Government is willing to pay 75 per cent of the cost of creating new child care spaces. That does not exist under CAP. I might explain that a bit further. This does not involve simply creating a brand new child care centre in a building. It means that if you have a child care centre which can perhaps accommodate only 12 children, and it wants to expand, then 75 per cent of the cost of improving that centre and creating additional spaces can be paid.
It also means that if a parent wants to spend her time with her child and has decided that she can help other mothers by taking children in, in other words an unlicensed facility, which the Hon. Member for Vancouver East has some concern about, that parent could apply to become a licensed centre and receive capital funding to add whatever is necessary to her home to turn it into a licensed child care facility. That is going one step further in that as a licensed facility she can provide receipts to the parent who will then be entitled to a tax deduction. It may mean putting a fence around the facility. It may mean adding an extra washroom in order to meet standards. Standards do exist. There has been discussion about whether standards exist. They do. In short, 75 per cent of the capital cost for expanding or creating facilities is available to the small entrepreneur, not necessarily just for the large child care centre.
By the same token, if someone comes forward and says they want to put in a 35 space child care centre they can draw up a business plan and under this legislation we could provide 75 per cent of the capital cost. I think that is very important to creating additional spaces.
Single parents are being looked after in a different way, too. A lot of parents, primarily single parents need assistance with parenting skills. In many cases they need someone to talk to. Under the $100 million initiative fund there are plans to help groups that can offer help in parenting skills.
Another thing that the capital dollars can be used for is toys. Many of these children come from single parent homes which do not have the funding and the children do not have toys. They need toys, including educational toys, to help develop their learning skills. The money can be spent to make sure there is a proper kind of educational toys not only in the larger centres but in the smaller family centres as well.
There is a lot there for the single parent and I am glad the Hon. Member asked me that question because I think it is important that it be clarified.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the motion of Mrs. Martin (p. 18222).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate at second reading of Bill C-144, principally because it is the most important piece of social legislation to come from the Government since it came to power in 1984. 1 am sorry that there is so much disagreement in this debate over a national child care program. All joking aside, this really should be a motherhood issue.
We all agree on the need for such a program. Using Health and Welfare Canada's own figures, there are over 850,000 children in this country under the age of six who have parents working more than 20 hours a week or who are studying full time. That enormous number of children are being served by just over 220,000 child care spaces at the present time. That is clearly inadequate.
Anyone just taking a cursory look at these figures can see that there is a crying need for child care right across the country. This problem is national in scope. Our children need care and their parents need our assistance. It is up to the federal Government to provide national leadership in dealing with this problem.
What has been the Government's response? It has come up with a program designed to create about 200,000 new spaces over a period of seven years. Clearly this will never meet the needs of over 850,000 children and their families. In fact, doubling the number of child care spaces over a period of seven years is a lower rate of growth than has been achieved without a national program. Child care spaces have doubled in just two years, from 1984 to 1986.
This raises a very relevant question. Why is the Government creating a program which is designed to fall far short of demand? Why start a program doomed to fail? If we are going to spend over $5 billion on child care, let us get it right the first time.
Let me touch me briefly on a few of the problems I see with the Government's proposal. In the first place, almost half the money for this proposal will not create new child care spaces. It is earmarked for tax expenditures. I thought we had realized in this country that tax expenditures are, in most cases, less
Canada Child Care Act
efficient than direct capital spending. It is hard to target a tax expenditure specifically.
Most of this $2.4 billion in tax expenditures will be used to double the child care tax deduction. This is clearly a regressive move. It does nothing to help the poor single parent. If one does not have enough income, one cannot take advantage of a tax deduction.
This measure flies in the face of tax reform as well. We are supposed to be moving from tax deductions to tax credits. Credits are also part of this patchwork quilt that the Government is calling a national program. Less well off families will get an increase of $100 in the child tax credit in each of the first two years. This is hopelessly inadequate. First, one cannot use this money to get child care if no spaces are available. One cannot break the cycle of poverty and dependence with a mere $200.
Conservatives are always saying that they want people to be self-reliant. But how can you get a single parent off welfare and into the workforce if the solution is to hand out $100 per year to hire a babysitter?
The real weakness of this measure can be seen when we compare it to the de indexing of things like family allowance that the Government has pushed through. It turns out that this measure will give back to Canadian families less than the $1.5 billion they will lose through de indexation. Inflation will eat up more than the Government is handing out.
What is most troubling about the Government's proposal is the lack of a set of national objectives and standards. There are no minimum standards of care established anywhere in this program.
We are discussing the needs of our children. They deserve adequate care. However, even this is not guaranteed by the Government's program.
We do not have to dictate terms to parents. We just simply must assure families that they can expect certain minimum standards of care for their children.
We just went through the debate on the Meech Lake Accord. It clearly says that national objectives can be set in such programs. Here is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate how our system of Confederation can work. We can establish a truly national program in an area of provincial jurisdiction.
Here is the perfect opportunity, moreover, for a federal Government to show some leadership. I see no leadership in this proposal. Instead, I am struck by the Government's curious lack of vision. Everyone can see the crying need for a national program. I have already outlined the figures. Where is the program that will meet the needs of our society?
It has been estimated that if all of the money used for things like tax expenditures had been used to create new child care spaces, we could create about 170,000 more spaces. That would at least be an add-on start.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
We have the opportunity to show that we understand the needs of average Canadian families. The Government could have shown that it understood their desire for quality affordable child care. Instead, we are fighting the same kind of battle we fought over deindexation. We have to show the Government that we have as much concern for the care of our children as we have for the security of our seniors.
This should also be a time to show our commitment to equality for women. We know that there are a lot of single parent families. Many of those families are headed by women. We know that single parents need affordable child care in order to work. We should be encouraging women to increase their participation in the labour force. We should show them that we want them to reach their full potential in society, but we should also realize that they will never achieve that potential if they are deprived of the opportunity to work because there are not enough child care spaces in Canada.
This proposal will not give them any choice, and the Government is simply not being open and honest about that. This program will not meet their needs.
Just as it fails in quantity, it also fails in quality. Instead of an affordable national program of quality child care with minimum standards, the Government is offering this patchwork, piecemeal approach. Instead of demonstrating a commitment to fairness for Canadian families, the Government is offering a program which is not even designed to meet their needs.
Instead of showing a vision of Canada where all its citizens can reach their full potential, the Government is content to throw money at the problem in a pre-election period. Incidentally, the fact that the Government wants to move with what I would call indecent haste, in trying to get this Bill through second reading after we have been debating it for just three hours at most, is totally unacceptable. As I said at the outset, this is the most important single piece of social legislation to come forward from the Government after it has been in power for almost exactly four years. Yet, in four hours, it wants to get this through second reading, out of the House, and into committee. There is absolutely no justification for this kind of haste at this time, election or no election on the horizon.
Canadians are not going to be fooled. They know this program is inadequate and should be rejected in its present form. It is a dilemma for all Members of Parliament who are opposed in principle to the mechanics of this Bill, or to its technical aspects, in view of the fact that child care and money for child care is very important. Nevertheless, there is no point in starting out on a national program unless we have the very best program we can put into place at the outset. If we do not have a good program with national standards and objectives, we may very well be wasting a lot of that $6.4 billion.
What should be put in its place? Canadian families should have access to a comprehensive, flexible and affordable system of child care. They need to know their children are safe and
secure while they are out earning a living. Children should not have to stay at home watching television all day with some well-intentioned teenager who is simply not qualified to assist, train, educate or care for those children. That means we have to put money into creating spaces in non-profit community organizations, not tax expenditures. This would give parents a voice in the kind of care their children receive. It would also allow us to guarantee quality. We should make funding to the provinces conditional on compliance with a set of minimum national standards and objectives.
I realize that such a system cannot be set up overnight, but in the meantime we should provide a series of good faith grants to the provinces. That way we can get started on the road to meeting the needs of Canadian families while we negotiate cost sharing with the provincial Governments. We must also be flexible. We have to realize that not everyone will have access to this type of child care. This is of particular concern to our remote or rural communities.
Parents should have the choice of going to licensed home care. That is why the Government should also fund home services which meet national standards. In that way it can ensure that facilities in these homes are adequate. This would give Canadian families real choices. They would no longer have to worry about the level of care their children receive. Canadian families need a comprehensive system of child care. They want a system that is fair for all families regardless of where they live or how much money they earn. They need to know their children will be safe and secure in the child care system. We should, therefore, reject the Government's proposal and get on with the job of meeting the real needs of Canadian families.
Let us show Canadian families that we understand their needs and have the vision to meet them. We are not opposed to the private sector being involved in child care. However, we argue that public funding should not be used to assist the private sector. If it wants to be in the business community and its job is child care, then let the market determine, through profit and loss, the quality of care for the children of its clients. We are not opposed to that. But we are opposed to, on the one hand, a lack of national standards and, on the other hand, giving money to private sector child care homes or institutions, which we feel is not fair to the taxpaying public of Canada. If the private sector wants to run a private operation, this is a free country, let it do so.
Also, based on the evidence that came before the committee, I would argue that non-profit child care is much more efficient and is of a higher quality of child care, generally speaking- and there are exceptions-across Canada.
In closing, I want to cast my mind back to some of the other great battles that have been fought in this Chamber in terms of bringing forward progressive social legislation. I can recall the critics, and most of them were either large C Conservative or small c conservative, when Tommy Douglas and Woodrow Lloyd brought in OHIP and medicare in the Province of
August 11, 1988

Saskatchewan. They said it could not be done. They said it would be wasteful. They said the Government had no business being in the medical care delivery system. They said it would be a great encroachment upon the private sector in what, in those days, was a market-driven medical care system. I do not think there is a Conservative or Liberal left in this country today who would want to go back to the pre-medicare system.
We are the envy of many progressive-thinking U.S. Senators and Members of the House of Representatives. I do not think I am quoting Michael Dukakis out of context when 1 repeat what I heard him say a couple of weeks ago in Atlanta. They would dearly love to have our medicare system in the United States, and one thing he said that night with respect to medicare was that 38 million Americans have no medical coverage at all and that he would initiate and bring in a medical care system similar to ours to cover those 38 million.
Those of us who fought the medicare battle some 25 years ago were considered radicals, unacceptable to the so-called market-driven medical care delivery system we had in those days, but today, I would argue, there are very few Canadians, rich, middle-income or low-income, who would want to get rid of that system.
I can recall a time, towards the end of the Diefenbaker period, when a professor of my university was called upon to head a commission of Mr. Diefenbaker's Conservative Government to find out whether or not it was financially viable to bring in a Canada pension system. After several months of hearings here in Ottawa and across the country, the conclusion was, no, this country could not afford a Canada Pension Plan as was being put forward at that time by the New Democratic Party and the Liberals. They said the country could not afford it and it would infringe upon the Great West Lifes of this country, the insurance companies that had it all wrapped up in their tidy little hands. We all know that when it comes to life insurance companies, if one reads the fine print one will find that the exclusionary language in almost every life insurance policy is appalling, to say nothing of the fact it is downright misleading. We fought that battle and finally got the Canada Pension Plan. Now we come to a national child care program.
I am arguing this evening that perhaps for some old fashioned thinkers in this House we are being a little too progressive or aggressive. I want Members in the House to think back to the medicare fight and the Canada pension fight, just those two issues, before we proceed much further with this Bill. Members will find that what we are arguing for and promoting is not perfect by any means, but we are moving in the right direction. There is no more precious commodity-if 1 can put it in those crass words-than our young people. Regardless of background, education or family income, unless they are all give an equal start in life, an equal opportunity to develop, the waste that will continue in this country will be inestimable. All one has to do is to look at those countries where child care and day care are virtually tied up in the private sector, where there are very few, if any, public
Canada Child Care Act
programs. You will find that if one is born in a black ghetto, or a hispanic ghetto in the United States, or a poor white ghetto, one does not have nearly the opportunity to develop as a young human being that one would have if one were born into a middle-income family or upper-income family.
We do not want that type of society in this country. We want to give all our kids an equal start in life and an equal opportunity. They may not all have equal qualities or capabilities, but the very least we can do is to provide them with an equal chance to get started.

I would like to congratulate my colleague on his remarks. He mentioned early in his remarks that, in his view, rather than having tax measures that were regressive and would take money that was very much needed for child care services, having regressive tax measures, and also having a tax credit of $100 for the first year and $200 thereafter for families not using licensed care, it would have been better for the Government to have reindexed the family allowance. Would the Hon. Member elaborate on that a little? Does the Hon. Member consider that the Government should have reindexed the child tax credit which would have targeted lower income families and, as the years went on, would also have increased upward the income range eligible for the child tax credit? These are two things that have been detrimental to families that have put particular economic pressure on low and average income families and contradict any family policy goals that the Government espouses.

In response to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), this is an extremely important aspect of this Bill. A tax deduction favours a few, or favours those who are earning higher incomes. To a considerable extent those on lower incomes are excluded, and those not paying any income tax at all because their incomes are so low are entirely neglected.
In order to make a policy or program like this fair and equitable, in my view there is only one way to do it, and that is by direct funding and making whatever the program is directly accessible to those individuals and their children. The minute tax policy is used in order to pay in part for any social program, literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians are excluded, or those with higher incomes are favoured.
In terms of raising the income cap, it is a well known fact that the heaviest portion of the tax burden in our country falls not on the rich, not on the poor, but on those in the middle-income area from $25,000 up to $40,000 a year. Those people in our society are becoming terribly fed up with having to bear a substantial burden, more than their fair share of taxation. These are very important aspects of this Bill. We feel that we have to reject those aspects of the funding as being unfair, inequitable, and not working in the best interests of all Canadians.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act

Could the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) outline how the Conservative Government has completely misled the people of Canada on this particular legislation, and how it has limited the number of day care spaces that will be created? I appreciate the speech made by the Hon. Member for Brant, and I know he can outline how the people of Canada have been misled on the number of spaces that have been created for young people in this country.

I appreciate that question very much. I am very happy that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) has come in to listen to my speech this evening. It is the first opportunity I have had to stand across from him and deliver a speech, although I have heard his speeches on many occasions.
Referring to what is misleading, when people take a look at the total sum that the Government is talking about they think that that is a total cash outlay of some $6.4 billion almost overnight as it were. Second, somehow this will automatically jump up the number of child care places to accommodate the total need. We all know that that is not the case.
I am not prepared to say that the Government is deliberately misleading the people in this regard. I leave it to the people to read the legislation, to read what is in the Bill, and to come to their own conclusion. I am quite sure that they will come to the same conclusion as my hon. friend from Comox-Powell River has come to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my friend the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) expressed gratitude that I would be down to listen to his speech. When I heard the Member for Brant was speaking on child care I immediately rushed to the House. I was up in my office working and I rushed to the House, because when I saw the astounding miracle that he had worked on the NDP defence policy, I could hardly wait to see what was going to happen on child care.
Both make a lot of sense too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I thank my distinguished friend for his welcome. I am always delighted to listen to his contributions to an important matter.
I rise, Mr. Speaker, with great pride to join in this historic debate on the Canada Child Care Act. In government we all have two general goals: to try to build a productive economy, and to try to build a caring society. These objectives are by no means mutually exclusive. Indeed, in many ways they are complementary and result in a nation hopefully that is more civilized and more prosperous.
First, I know that all Members of the House, irrespective of political Party, will join with me in saluting the tremendous leadership role of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for bringing forward child care and fostering a national consensus on a very important matter.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I gather the NDP is holding its applause for a little later.
A lot later.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I think that the national consensus engendered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and by the Minister responsible for the Status of Women on the four principal objectives of availability, accessibility, affordability, and above all, quality, has been a commendable achievement, and on behalf of all Members of the House I want to underline his tremendous contribution to our national well-being.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
As a result of this initiative we will be allocating $6.4 billion over seven years, creating 200,000 new quality spaces and virtually doubling the number of spaces available today. That strikes me, irrespective of Party, of being a major contribution to the national well-being of Canada, and I would think that all parliamentarians would want to celebrate that fact.
In so doing we are honouring an important commitment that I made on behalf of my Party during the last election campaign. At the First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver in 1986 I said that one of the most important factors contributing to the persistent and persisting inequality of women in this country is the lack of affordable, flexible, quality child care. We have been determined from the beginning of our mandate to seek to create and implement a national child care program worthy of the name. With this Bill I believe that we are in the process of doing just that.

And in the process, Mr. Speaker, we are preparing Canada for the social and economic challenges of a new decade and a new century. Consider the following: Today, more than half of Canadian mothers with young children are in the work force. The Canada child Care Act, with its emphasis on flexibility, will help facilitate choices in child care. We want parents, and this is something you tend to forget, we want parents to be able to choose the kind of child care best suited to their values and their requirements. We recognize that there are different needs in each family just as there are different needs in various regions, from British Columbia to Newfoundland and Labrador.
The demands of adequate child care, say in Williams Lake, British Columbia, clearly differ from those required in Burlington, Ontario, or in Rimouski, Quebec. But the fundamental objective, we believe, is the same everywhere, to give all Canadian mothers the possibility of going to work, secure in the knowledge that their children are in clean, safe and supportive surroundings. The Canada Child Care Act is about protecting children, about helping parents, about strengthening the Canadian family. Most of all, we want the best of care for our future generations.
August 11, 1988

We are living in an era of remarkable economic and social change. These are challenging times, but they can be rewarding for Canadians individually and for our society as a whole. Some 56 per cent of Canadian women are in the workforce today, as compared with 45 per cent in 1976, and 35 per cent a decade earlier, in 1966.
It is a matter of particular pride for me that of the nearly
1,300,000	new jobs created since I had the honour of being sworn in as Prime Minister, fully 728,000, or 56 per cent of all of those jobs, have gone to women in Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: That is a spectacular growth rate of 15.5 per cent in women's employment in less than four years, as compared, for example, to 8.8 per cent for men. That means that the number of women's jobs has been growing almost twice as fast as the number of new jobs for men. That is catchup. There has been a growing demand and an historic injustice, and the policies of the Government are important economically. I am proud to be associated with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in this. The economic policies of the Government have made an important social statement, and these figures indicate that Canadian women, having been left behind for so many years, are now playing catch-up and getting their fair share of economic jobs and equality of opportunity in Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Of that growth in women's jobs, 78 per cent, more than three-quarters, have been full-time jobs, reversing almost completely the trend under the previous Government, where employment for women was essentially part-time. The unemployment rate for women has declined from 12 per cent to 8.4 per cent, a decline of nearly one-third in less than four years. I think that all Members of the House would agree that this is a happy development for all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
The number of women employed in managerial and administrative positions has grown by 36 per cent between 1984 and 1987.
These are strong indicators, not perfect, but strong and vigorous indicators, that we are moving in the right direction as a country, that we are moving towards fairness and equity for women. We are guided by these principles of fairness and equity as we prepare for the societal changes of the next decade.
If you look anywhere across Canada, at our universities, you can see the dimensions of the winds of change that are about to sweep across this country. Women account for nearly half, and
Canada Child Care Act
in some areas more than half, of the enrolment in our faculties of medicine and law and business.

In Quebec, especially in business administration and international trade, more and more women are outdistancing men in so-called traditional jobs or careers.

This is a major development. Women have moved as well into small business in a very big way. Women accounted for 95 per cent of the net increase in unincorporated small businesses between 1980 and 1985. The number of self-employed women grew by 118 per cent between 1975 and 1986.

With these changes to the face of our economy, there has been a strong and positive evolution in attitudes during the present decade. What used to be known primarily as women's issues are now called, quite properly-and I think the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) will agree-society's issues.
Child care is such an issue. It is about social justice, but it is equally about economic justice. In terms of social justice, we want Canadian mothers to be able to participate in the work force if they choose, to the degree they wish to do so, to expand their own horizons, to develop their own capacities, to enhance their own prosperity and to pursue their own dreams. At the same time, we also want to respect the decision of those mothers who choose to remain at home to raise their children.
That is why this important and historic initiative is based on the fundamental principle of choice.

Freedom of choice, this is what this is all about. This is not a unitary, uniform, homogenized society. There are different people with different dreams and different options, and this gives Canadian women freedom of choice.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
This initiative recognizes the needs of both women with children who work outside the house and women with children who choose to work at home with their children.
Canada has long been a world leader in promoting social justice for its citizens. From the time of the baby bonus in the 1940s and Old Age Security in the fifties, down to the Canada-Quebec Pension Plans and medicare in the sixties, Canada has been well regarded in the international community for its by and large generous and civilized approach to social programs across the country.
I believe and I hope that Members of the House from all sides will agree with me. I hope that perhaps a decade from now, a generation hence, the Canada Child Care Act will be

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
regarded as perhaps the most important social innovation in the 1980s.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Our critics-and there are a few here in the House-say that the child care program is-
Very few.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Well, the Member from Brant is saying very few. He is very right.
Sixty-six per cent of Canadians.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I think, measured by any standard, all Members would agree that $6.4 billion is a substantial sum of money. By contrast, and to put it into some perspective, consider the debate, for example, on child care in the United States of America, in the general election that will soon take place. Vice-President George Bush, the Republican nominee for President, has proposed a $2.2 billion package of tax credits for low-income families. Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic nominee, has proposed a $2.5 billion program for the children of working parents.
Jesse Jackson.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: That is in a country with 10 times our population.
Don't use them as an example. They have the worst child care program in the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: We are proposing for Canadians a $6.4 billion program over seven years, and I think that that is a great tribute to Canada and its notion of justice for working women.
Hear, hear!
How about comparing it to Sweden, Holland, Norway, Denmark, France, Italy, Germany?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I believe that those figures tend to put the debate in a different and, I think, quite interesting perspective. We are doing this, which is very important, within the fiscal framework of responsibility that the Minister of Finance introduced in November, 1984, and which-may I say to his great credit and because of his very, very significant leadership-this Government has respected ever since and will in the future.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
There is a very important economic and social reason for this, Mr. Speaker. It is not being hung on a given concept of deficit reduction. There is a very important reason of social justice associated with this. The notions of deficit reduction and social programs are not at variance one with the other.

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, our program of financial restraint and our economic policies have encouraged sufficient growth in the economy that we are able to afford this important, most historic initiative. It must not be forgotten that when we assumed office, the deficit was at $38 billion and ticking like a time bomb. We have defused that. Less than four years later, the deficit has been reduced by nearly $10 billion a year, and we are right on target for reducing our borrowing requirements by half over five years. I think this is a most significant achievement for any Government of Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
We began, Mr. Speaker, from the premise that Canadians needed more work. We began from the principle that governments don't create wealth, people do.

Governments do not create wealth. Governments can, however, create conditions within which new wealth can be generated by Canadian citizens, by the genius of the entrepreneurial spirit, by the risk-takers who create jobs, by those who have vision and believe in job creation. Governments cannot create those themselves but they can create conditions conducive to that kind of economic growth if they get their spending down, as we have, if they get their deficits down, as we have done, if they encourage, not discourage, investment if they attract investment and in the process attract jobs, and if they reduce regulatory constraint to economic growth, as we have tried to do from the very beginning of our mandate. The result of this, Mr. Speaker, has been lower interest rates, which has produced sustained growth in a climate-controlled inflation.
The 1.3 million new participants in our economy today resulting from new jobs created are paying into our envelope of social programs rather than drawing from it.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Canadians are now themselves with their own hard earned money, rather than with borrowed money that does not last and is shoved on to the backs of our young and new generation, creating a broader and a deeper national pool of new wealth. It is based on that new wealth that the Government and the people of Canada provide the kinds of programs and social justice, such as the national child care program that is before the House of Commons today.
I think that by creating an additional 200,000 quality child care spaces many more mothers will have an opportunity to participate in the labour force.
While this is very much about social justice, it is equally about economic justice.

August 11, 1988

[ Translation]
And in the strictest economic terms, we cannot hope to achieve our economic potential in the 1990s wihtout the full and fully engaged participation of as many Canadians as possible who wish to enter the job market.
In the coming decade, we will have to make some real economic and social choices for this country. We will need, for example, more qualified immigrants, not fewer, if we are to sustain our economic growth. We will need a more literate labour force. It is, in both human and economic terms, a terribly sad fact that one Canadian adult in four is functionally illiterate. In the coming era of technological change, in a time when research and development must be a national hallmark of excellence, we must have a work force whose skills are fully developed and whose potential is fully realized. I think those are some of the dimensions of the economic and social challenges that we will face in the coming decade.

And so, Mr. Speaker, in a very special way the constant challenge for a civilized and tolerant Government is to be, as best it can, formed, as any Government is, of human beings with their own imperfections, both competent and caring. For without the prudent management of our nation's fiscal resources we cannot free up new resources on the social side to meet the increasing demands of an increasingly complex society. We all know that it requires that kind of growth and new wealth to meet the constant demand of society. So it is a matter of some pride to the members of this Government that we have been able to expand our social framework within a fiscal framework of some considerable restraint.
Many of these issues are of special concern to women and to working mothers, but not exclusively. They affect all of us. In a very special way, they have a particular effect on women and working mothers. We have sought to respond to a number of them in constructive ways, for example, the spousal allowances. One of our first acts in government was to extend spousal allowances to all low-income widows and widowers aged 60 to 64. This increased income protection to about
50,000	widows and provided some $200 million in additional benefits. We introduced improvements to the Canada Pension Plan with an improved benefits package, including an early retirement option, increased disability benefits and improved pension benefits for women, which benefited about 230,000 Canadian women. We have increased fourfold our assistance to disabled persons' organizations. The tax changes from the first Budget changing the definition of disability have resulted in increased benefits for another 85,000 Canadians.
On drug abuse, which affects us all but in a special way affects mothers who are charged with the responsibility and the heartache that comes from the impact of this situation, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has brought in a $200 million five-year strategy to curb this tragic situation which afflicts not only our youth but all professional and income levels of our society.
Canada Child Care Act
In a major CBC news report a few weeks ago Dr. Ivan Porosko, director of a cocaine treatment program in Toronto, described cocaine abuse in Canada as an epidemic, a most interesting choice of words, with which most mothers in Canada would agree. They are asking the Government of Canada to get rid of this savage problem which weakens our family and debilitates our country.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
In the very sad and tragic area of battered women, we are creating 500 new shelter units which can accommodate an additional 25,000 women and children per year.
On child abuse, the Government has enacted Bill C-115 which addresses in a substantive manner the sexual abuse and exploitation of children.
With regard to native women, about which demands have been made in this House of Commons year after year, and many members of the NDP raised this with Conservatives when we were together in the Opposition, I am honoured to say and to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that we introduced amendments to the Indian Act which replaced discriminatory elements and gave back aboriginal women both status and band membership, thereby benefiting 10,000 native women in Canada.
No money to house them.
No resources.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
We have introduced amendments to the Criminal Code to ensure that victims of crime are given increased attention in the criminal courts, and we have secured agreement from the provinces and territories on a statement of principles for victims.
Regarding the proceeds of crime, we have instituted procedures to seize, freeze and forfeit the proceeds of crime. At the request of all Members of this House, we have imposed stiffer penalties for impaired driving and established new provisions for mandatory blood testing.
In a very important social problem area, the question of AIDS research, we have introduced a $ 129-million initiative for research, public awareness and education and community services. Perhaps we cannot reduce the pain and suffering of AIDS victims, but we can remove the social stigma which is attached to it and we can concentrate and ensure that more and more resources go to the research so that we can find a cure for this debilitating and unfair disease which affects so many people in Canada.
This, I think, is a solid record of achievement of which all Members of this Parliament can be proud. It indicates that this Government has provided strong and improved social programs that go hand in hand with economic renewal, and the child care program is but the most recent illustration of that.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
There are those who argue that this can be done in a vacuum, that this can be done with borrowed money, that this can be done overnight while raising the deficit and driving up interest rates. There are even those who argue that Canada's social, cultural and environmental programs will, for example, be adversely affected by a free trade agreement with the United States of America. Elowever, in the final analysis, action speaks louder than unfounded fears.
In the last nine months, our Government has, among other things, passed a tough new Environmental Protection Act, the most comprehensive environmental legislation among the leading industrialized nations-
Order, order!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: We have renewed the Official Languages Act for the first time in 17 years. We have acted to provide copyright protection to Canadian artists and musicians. We have established the first ever legislative recognition of Canada's multicultural heritage-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: And if you don't like to hear it, we're going to repeat it again.
Hear, hear!

So it might be ... This is a point of order. I think that he should talk about something to do with day care, not crime, drinking, pensions, etc. He is out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I accept the Hon. Member's intervention. [English]
Perhaps I can just say that I know that the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would know that during some parts of his speech, there seemed to be some agitation on the other side, I think aimed at the question of relevance. I would ask the Right Hon. Prime Minister to keep that in mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I apologize to my hon. friend who takes offence at some of the important questions that we are discussing. I have always thought that the Canadian family and the needs of the Canadian family involved day care, but also all of the other important matters that were unaddressed for 20 years and that this Government has now dealt with.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, among other things, we have introduced the $6.4-billion child care program that we are
debating today. These are the actions of a Government determined to strengthen Canada's social, environmental and cultural programs, and in our judgment they are all linked together. They cannot be cut off one from the other. They go to the well-being of families, they go to the well-being of working mothers, they go to the well-being of Canadian who need jobs, and all of them must be considered together. Only a Liberal would believe that you could cut off one from the other. There must be a program but there must be a way to pay for it, and that is why we believe in a strong economy.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
They are the actions of a Government determined to lead in implementing coherent national programs.

These actions clearly illustrate that this Government is committed to social justice for all Canadians. Child care is the centrepiece of that commitment. We embark on this initiative with pride and with confidence. We have every reason to believe that this program will work well and respond to the needs and aspirations of a vibrant, modern Canada. Years from now, when historians are assessing our stewardship of the country, I hope that they will say that this initiative in particular provided substantial benefits for Canadian women.

I hope it will be said that we in this Parliament developed the right social and economic initiatives for the times. I hope it will be recorded that we strengthened the social future of Canada and that our years were marked by a certain generosity of spirit, that all of us worked together on the fundamental issues to build a more tolerant society.
I have been somewhat taken with the fact that members of the Opposition seem to believe that Canada, Canadian women and Canadian families do operate in a vacuum, that child care can be segregated from drug abuse, from drunken driving, from the absence of jobs. I am being asked whether this fits together and whether we have done something.
I stand today before a Party that for 20 years had the pleasure and the privilege of sitting here talking about child care but which never once fulfilled its responsibilities to the family. I stand before you, Mr. Speaker, and say that the women of Canada understand that with the creation of 1.3 million new jobs, 56 per cent of those jobs have gone to working women, and that is a tremendous contribution to social justice for all the women of Canada.
Most of all, I think it will be recorded that the child care initiative that has been brought forward today, representing billions of dollars, recognizes and understands a commitment

August 11, 1988

to justice, fairness and equality for Canadian women. This is what the Parliament of Canada is all about.
There are cheers from the children in the gallery.

speechtext: You're making the kids cry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister

A seven-month-old baby understands, but the Liberals don't. I could say that that was a loud and ringing endorsement from one of the principal beneficiaries of the child care program.
I think all of us can take pride in the fact that for the first time a national child care program has been brought forward which will double in a period of years the number of spaces available to women and their children, thereby strengthening the most important element of our society, which is the Canadian family.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: It happens all the time.
When was the last time Turner answered a question?

The fact is that the Prime Minister did not respect the rules of relevance and the Speaker got up to remind him of that fact. For a good half of his speech he did not speak on the Bill before us.
As I said, he had his swan song and I hope historians will record it as such, as his last speech in this House, and that he will be remembered, unfortunately, by Canadian historians as the Prime Minister who weakened Canadian federalism and virtually sold Canada to the Americans. That will be the sad legacy he leaves behind.
He also raised a number of rhetorical balloons, so to say, and they must be punctured one by one, because this is a place for debate and a rebuttal is perfectly in order.
The fact is that the Prime Minister got carried away in his rhetoric. He seemed to imply that only as of 1984 have women entered the labour force in increasing numbers. That is not true. That trend was set in place long before the election of 1984. Certainly no one will take that theology as a fact.
After four years in power women are still earning 65 cents for every dollar men earn. The Government has done nothing to correct that imbalance. The Prime Minister implied that enrolment of women in universities has been increasing under the present regime. We know very well that the enrolment of our female population in universities has been increasing for a number of years. It has nothing to do with who is in power.
The Prime Minister would like the public to believe that the number of self-employed women and women owners of unincorporated businesses is on the increase as a result of the Tory Government. That is sheer nonsense. This trend has taken place for a number of reasons and certainly not because a particular Party is in power in Ottawa. That development has nothing to do with what happened in September of 1984.
The Prime Minister made a big item of freedom of choice, which is a codified manner of excusing to the public the fact that the Bill which we are debating tonight will not set national standards for child care. That is what he means when he speaks about freedom of choice, and the public ought to know that. The Prime Minister referred several times to the fact that over the next seven years $6.4 billion will be made available for child care. In reality it is $4 billion, and I will return to that later.
The Prime Minister compared the Canadian measure to what Vice-President Bush is proposing in the United States, which is $2.2 billion, and to what democratic presidential candidate Dukakis has proposed, which is $2.5 billion. Well, so what? Since when does Canada take its lead from the Americans on social policy? Is that now becoming the bench-mark for the quality and standard that we want for Canadians? Is that where the Prime Minister takes his inspiration for what Canadians should be given?
The Prime Minister referred to the time bomb of the deficit. Those are his own words. Well, the time bomb imposed by the deficit was conveniently forgotten in the weeks and days preceding the last by-election. At that time the deficit did not exist. Why is it that when we approach a by-election and a general election, as we now are, the Government spends like a drunken sailor? It has been estimated that in the time leading up to the by-election and in subsequent weeks the Government spent $14 billion in commitments and promises leading to the fall of 1988.
The Prime Minister made reference to the prudent management of our nation's resources. He is very proud that he is capable, therefore, to offer this measure. I would like the Prime Minister and each Tory Member to address themselves to the estimated expenses of projects proposed in the White Paper on defence as compared to what the Government is proposing for child care. The Prime Minister should do that before he has the nerve to talk about the prudent management of our national resources. I will return to that in a moment.
The fact is that in the four years of the Government's mandate, low-income families earning up to $25,000 a year have seen their taxes increased by 22 per cent. That is what the Tory Government has done in the last four years. The fact is that the Government attempted to deindex senior citizens' pensions. It was stopped but it tried in 1985, didn't it? The fact

August 11, 1988

is that the Government was successful, unfortunately, in deindexing family allowances. It was successful in deindexing the child tax credit. Is that the prudent management to which the Prime Minister referred? Does the Parliamentary Secretary agree with that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Yes.

The fact is that, as a result of Bill C-22, there has been an increase in the cost of drugs which will mainly affect senior citizens. Is that prudent management by the Tory Government? The fact is that, with regard to the production of social and co-operative housing, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has virtually been put on ice. Those are the facts in reply to the rhetoric of the Prime Minister.
Contrary to the impression the Prime Minister has attempted to create in this House, we have had fine legislation by the name of the Canada Assistance Plan since 1966. That was introduced in the Pearson years. The Prime Minister seems never to have heard of that. Under the Canada Assistance Plan we laid the foundation for all the fine social measures which exist today, including the measure which makes it possible today to have the basic minimum in child care.
That brings me to the substance of this Bill which is, in a way, a deathbed repentance by the Government in its fourth year in government. I intend to make eight points which will make the life of the Parliamentary Secretary rather unpleasant.
First, the measure before us provides for only one-seventh of the child care spaces which are being requested by the provinces over the next seven years. It is estimated that 1.4 million child care spaces are required in our society. This Bill provides for 200,000 only. That fact is established by the projections of the provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: What nonsense. You are totally wrong.

The Parliamentary Secretary's ignorance is so visible. He need only do his homework. Having offered one-seventh of the requirement for the next seven years as proposed by the provinces and the two Territories, the Government has imposed a ceiling on each province. I will use as an example the Province of Ontario from which both the Parliamentary Secretary and I come. The imposition of the ceiling under this Bill in Ontario will mean a reduction in Ontario's plan for child care by some 12,000 spaces. That is my second point.
Third, this measure would build fewer child care spaces in Canada over the next seven years than would be possible under the existing legislation because of the ceiling to which I made reference a moment ago.
Fourth, it was very revealing that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), in his speech this morning, avoided committing the Government to the establishment of national standards in child care. This measure would allow for the balkanization of this important social program and will prove right those who oppose the Meech Lake agreement and
Canada Child Care Act
said that there would never be another national social program. Bill C-144 proves that. We will have different standards in each province. That is the net effect of the wording of the legislation.
The Minister carefully avoided the words "national standards" in his speech because he knows very well that that is the fact. Each province will go its own way and there will be no national standards on child care. The Government has no guts and no political will to set national standards. We saw the same situation with Bill C-74, the Environmental Protection Act. This is the same pattern and it is what I call the Meech Lake virus.
Fifth, this Bill does not set priorities. The net effect will be that the needs of the most disadvantaged parents will not be taken into account as a result of lack of priority. As my colleague, the Member for Outrement (Mrs. Pepin), pointed out in her excellent speech earlier today, this Bill will make things more difficult for needy parents.
Sixth, this Bill completely ignores the existence of latchkey kids. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary knows what latchkey kids are. He has a limited knowledge of social affairs. I will explain to him what latchkey kids are. They are the kids who go to school with a key around their neck. He has probably never seen them. They do exist in large numbers in west Toronto where I come from. This Bill ignores completely the fact that after a certain hour kids come home to an empty house. A measure like that in this Bill would have been the ideal vehicle to address that particular social need.

My next point deals with the situation in Davenport where we have consulted a number of day care centres this morning. I was given some interesting statistical background. For instance, we were informed that the average waiting list at the Dovercourt Boys and Girls Club is some 15 people. This is one of many day care centres in Toronto. There is a great potential for expansion, which this Bill will hardly be able to meet.
