The waiting list is one and a half years at the Dovercourt International Day Care Service. The average waiting list at the Elarmony Day Nursery is 100 to 120 children. The waiting list for special needs children at the MacAulay child development centre is 30 names. The average waiting list is 20 children in the case of the Old Davenport Child Centre. At the Sister Regina Mass Day Nursery, the average waiting list is 35 to 36 children. The waiting period can be fairly long. In the case of St. Chad's Day Nursery, the average waiting list is at least 20 names. Time does not permit me to cover them all.
Let me conclude with the comparison of the Government's priorities. This measure offers $4 billion over the next seven years plus a total of S2.3 billion in tax credits.
Let us compare the priority the Government gives to kids with its priority on defence equipment projects over the next 10 years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: It is 27 years.

I will make it 10 years to make it easier for the Parliamentary Secretary to understand. On the one hand, the Government is offering our kids in direct funds, $4 billion over the next seven years, while on the other hand, there is the following breakdown in Tory defence equipment projects over the next 10 years: $8 billion for nuclear powered submarines; $12 billion for ship borne helicopters over five years; $2.7 billion for a second set of patrol frigates over nine years; $750 million for minesweepers over 10 years; $420 million over 10 years for all terrain troop carriers; $250 million for heavy trucks over approximately four years. The funding for tripling of reserve forces is $9.2 billion over 15 years. The battletanks yet to be announced will cost some $1.8 billion to $2.8 billion over the next five years.
The comparison is $4 billion toward a social program on child care versus that $25 billion. That is the priority and the prudent management, to which the Prime Minister referred a few minutes ago, of this so-called Progressive Conservative Government. What a sham.
What a disgrace that the Government would see less value in preparing the young generation under 14 years of age to grow up in our urban centres and in rural Canada by allocating $4 billion in the next seven years compared to $25 billion to be allocated to defence equipment projects. The Government believes that defence projects must have greater importance, because of our NATO commitment, than the value of our next generation. I find that a form of pornography of power and reverse priority that one could ever see in the history of our country. It is disgraceful and shameful.
If the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare said today that his measure takes into account all of the requirements of the provinces and the 1.4 million kids for the next seven years, my comparison would have lost its meaning and its impact. I would be the first to admit it. Such a measure would have taken into account the requirements of the provinces and the
Territories. Instead, the Minister came in with a measure that meets the needs of only one-seventh of our youth and their respective families. The conclusion is that this measure shows the bankruptcy in terms of social values and priorities of the Government, whose days are numbered. The sooner an election is called, the better.

Mr. Speaker, we know quite clearly that the Member who spoke is very much against the Bill that has been proposed. However, his Party is opposed to everything the Government has proposed, except Meech Lake. I think the Member himself opposes Meech Lake and therefore opposes everything the Government introduces. Perhaps that is a fault in our system.
We know what his Party opposes. We know that it supports the Senate and the unfettered rule of the Senate. Will he, without any personal attack, tell us what he would like to see in a day care plan and how much it would cost?

Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that the Hon. Member, for whom I have great respect, was not in the House when the Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) made the position of our Party quite clear. She established our Party's position point by point. She analysed for every aspect, and in much greater depth than I, what are the shortcomings and the alternatives that the Liberal Party of Canada would produce. That would take me much longer than the few minutes available to me.
However, they are on the record for everyone to see tomorrow in Hansard. They are also outlined in great detail in a document entitled Choices for Child Care: Now and the Future. I would be glad to supply the Hon. Member with a copy of this document which sets out a very positive Liberal approach to this matter. I know of his sincere interest in these matters.
Our basic position in principle is that we want to focus on the needy first. We would want to take into account the requirements of the low income and middle-income Canadians first as a major priority, to ensure that there is fairness built into the system. That has been the Liberal position on every social measure that has been adopted over the decades. That has been our guiding principle. This is what probably differs from the approach of the Progressive Conservative Government.
As I mentioned in my speech, this measure fails to take into account those youngsters who go home after school to an empty house because their parent or parents work. That is a very serious vacuum which we addressed in our interventions here today.
We also indicated that the requirements of Canadian society in 1988, because of the evolution in the family structure, particularly with respect to single parent families, are such
August 11, 1988

that a much larger number of families must be addressed. I think we have been pretty positive in our criticisms and in defining alternatives. In addition, I took the liberty of comparing the priorities of this Government in the over-all picture by addressing the amount of money that is being made available for this badly needed social measure compared to the Tory defence equipment projects over a parallel period of time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) about his new-found interest in day care. He has been a Member of this House for a number of years. He was in a previous Cabinet but I have never heard him talk about day care before. This is a revelation. Here is an individual who was in the Liberal Cabinet of Pierre Elliott Trudeau. He was, 1 must say, a less than effective Minister of the Environment. I never heard him talk about day care. I never heard him advocate day care. I did not see any day care programs whatsoever come out of that administration. I am glad the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) is sitting beside him, dropping, I am sure, some hints in his ear, because she understands the problem. I will give her full marks for that.
Great hypocrisy has been shown in the House tonight by the Hon. Member who talks about day care as if he has been an advocate in Davenport for years and years. He has never discussed it before. He has never debated it before. This is the first time he has ever stood up in the House of Commons and talked about day care. What a show of hypocrisy!
I might also point out that the statistics the Hon. Member talked about, comparing day care help and defence expenditures, was playing loose with the truth, and he knows it. The statistics he was giving were all selected figures, some spread over 20 years and some spread over 10 years. He knows full well that the submarine program this Government is talking about will cost the taxpayers of this country one-half of 1 per cent of the social spending in this country. For him to stand up and try to compare the day care figures with defence spending is a total fallacy, and he knows it. He is playing very loose with the truth.

Mr. Speaker, I am so glad I have touched a raw nerve. I am delighted to see the Parliamentary Secretary angry at being put into a corner to such an extent that all he can say about my intervention is to use the word "hypocrisy". He has run out of steam. He has no other argument. Out of sheer desperation he has to refer to my record as the Minister of the Environment. This is one of the most pathetic arguments I have heard because the record can be seen by anyone. It is just another example of Tory bankruptcy. When one has good ideas, one does not refer to hyprocrisy or former performances, but to the subject matter at hand. We are debating day care tonight.
I am sorry the Parliamentary Secretary did not like former Prime Minister Trudeau. He was a great Prime Minister. I am sorry the Parliamentary Secretary has no positive words to say about him. I served under him and I am proud of that fact. I
Canada Child Care Act
know there are millions of Canadians who would love to see Mr. Trudeau as Prime Minister of this country any time, any day, to replace the present, weak leader-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt. I have given a little more time than necessary, but I would like to cut it off right now. Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate.

Mr. Speaker, it was, of course, time to cut things off. When the spokesperson for the Liberal Party is hearkening back to the Trudeau era and is making it quite clear that he has no confidence in his present Leader, I think it is time to move on. I did have a question for him but I will ask it another day.
I want to zero in on this whole question of day care, I must say, quite in contrast to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) did in this House. He covered the waterfront. He talked about things that affect families, but he did not say a great deal about the legislation before us. His speech sounded very much like an election speech. I am surprised that at the end of his speech he did not announce he was going to see the Governor General. Perhaps he is on his way there now.
Day care has been in and out of the headlines of the newspapers for the last couple of years. When the Prime Minister was campaigning before the last election, he made big promises with respect to day care. We then had a couple of commissions and studies which took a look at day care, but the Government's program on day care kept being put off and put off. Finally the program was unveiled and made public. What stands out in my mind, and I am sure it stands out in the minds of most Canadians who observe what is going on in politics, is the headline which stated that the Government was going to spend $6.4 billion on day care. Coming from a Conservative Government this was a surprise because at first glance we had the impression that here was a Government doing something substantial, that here was a Government taking a step forward in the day care field, because $6.4 billion is a lot of money. It sounds like a lot of money and when it is spread across the headlines, one has to be impressed. The time for day care has arrived.
So I am not surprised if many Canadians, at least at this moment, think that the Government is doing something substantial in the area of day care. But if we step back a little from those headlines, from those billion dollar figures, and examine what the Government is doing, perhaps we will get a little perspective on the situation.
The first thing I want to point out is that, of course, it is necessary to make real advances in the area of day care in order to meet the kinds of needs which have emerged over the last couple of decades. We must first begin by comparing the Government's program for day care with the need in the community. If we accept at face value the Government's indication that its program over seven years will produce some

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
200,000	new day care spaces, clearly that will be an improvement. However, my understanding is that there will still be a couple of million children who will require day care spaces. In other words, the amount of day care spaces being provided is nowhere near what is needed. We can debate the amount of need that exists in the community. We can debate whether all children should be in day care centres. We can debate whether most mothers would prefer to stay home and take care of their children rather than working and having to send their children to day care.
When we use statistics to point out the size of the need in the country some government Members accuse us of being social engineers, or of wanting to regiment society and shove every child into day care. However, in spite of those political points that are being made, and even though those political points may be effective in some quarters, or perhaps are persuasive to some people, it does not erase the reality that the amount of spaces that will be created by the day care program of the Government in no way matches the need.
Over the last two decades increasing numbers of women and increasing numbers of mothers have entered the labour force. Therefore, there is a social revolution. Rather than things being as they once were where the father would be in the workforce and the mother would be at home with the children, this situation has changed radically. If one looks at the statistics, it can be seen that the number of families in which the mother stays home rather than works as well as takes care of the children is in the minority today. For the majority of families the social reality is that both parents are working.
When both parents work we as a society must ask the fundamental questions: "How do we take care of our children? How do we take care of young Canadians? How do we assure ourselves that young children receive the loving, adequate, and competent care that they require in order that they will grow up to be good people, competent, mature individuals, and good citizens?" That is what the day care question is about. It is about the making of mature and responsible human beings.
It is important to note that there are many families in which both parents are working and there is a need for quality care for those children. Those children should not be cared for as a happenstance. The Government has stated that it is spending $6.4 billion on day care. While that makes a big splash and a big impression, the impact on the social reality is a fraction of what is needed. First, that is over seven years, therefore, there is less than $1 billion a year. This is a fast emerging social need that demands a radical restructuring of our spending priorities so that we can find the resources necessary in order to provide the services.
If we put the day care program of the Government in the light of what is required and needed then it falls short of the mark. Some people might say that that is okay because we are making some progress and while some people would like to go faster, we are going as fast as we can.
If we compare what the Government is doing with what is needed, we might accept that as a perspective and as a way of
looking at and evaluating the day care program of the Government. If a much more thorough analysis is conducted of the Government's day care program, for example, a budgetary analysis, and we compared the program against what is needed and what was in place already, if we compared the budget for day care that exists today under the Canada Assistance Plan, which has present legislation, budgets, and a track record, with the program the Government is bringing forward now, the Epp program, and if we looked behind the headlines, we would find out something that is quite shocking because it radically changes our perspective on this program. If the present program for day care were left in place, the Canada Assistance Plan, there would be more day care spaces created over the next seven years than there will be under the initiative of the Government.
When I first heard that stated I was short of breath and knocked back. I could not believe it, because I had been reading the headlines and they gave me the impression that the Government was taking a bold initiative. However, when someone took the time to study the details of the program and its budget, they found out that the Government is replacing an existing day care program with a new program that will produce fewer day care spaces than the old program would have. We have a retreat on day care and a cut-back. There is a diminished commitment on day care. In fact, it begins to make a lot of sense. While it would be surprising to see a Conservative Government take bold action on day care, it makes a lot more sense when we understand that it is replacing a program that is in place with a new program that will cost less and produce fewer spaces. That fits much more with our experience of the Government.
When the Government has changed social policies over the last four years it has always meant a lower priority on the scale of social programs, and it has meant fewer dollars for social programs. For example, when the Government decided to do something about old age pensions, what did it do? When government Members spoke in the House they spoke of improvements, but what they attempted to foist on people was a deindexation of the old age pensions and removing the annual cost of living raises that go up with inflation. Over a period of years that would have destroyed the pensions. That is much more typical of the actions of the Government. The point that we must realize is that the Government is introducing a program that will have a less positive impact when it comes to day care than the program that is presently in place.
I wish to return to the question of day care from a different angle. What are the elements that make up a good day care program? I want to take some advice from people who have studied this very closely, particularly the women's organization, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women. It was established in 1973 as an independent organization funded by the federal Government. The Council's mandate is to advise the Government and inform the public on matters of concern to women.
August 11, 1988

This is what the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, who is there to advise Government on day care, says about child care. It ends up with a question, but it says this, that almost two million pre-school children across Canada need child care services because their parents work or study more than 20 hours a week. But there are only 244,000 licensed child care spaces to meet their needs. The federal Government's national child care strategy for the next seven years will do little to address the child care crisis. By 1995, at the end of the seven-year period, only 25 per cent of current need for licence spaces will be met. More than half of the funds allocated by the federal Government to child care during that time will give tax breaks to higher-income parents.
The proposed program will do little to make quality child care services available to all children and families who need it. It does not adequately recognize the contributions of parents who care for children at home.
That is the comment of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women on the Government's child care strategy. It ends up with a question that it would like to ask Members of Parliament and candidates in the next election, and that is: What steps will your Party take to ensure that publicly-funded, non-profit quality child care services are universally available to all families who need them in the same way that health and education now are?
That is the question that we have to ask the Government. What is it prepared to do to see that there are publicly-funded non-profit quality child care services, universally accessible, in the same manner as health and education? In other words, we would not tolerate a situation in which the vast majority of Canadian children did not have access to health care or did not have access to education, to schools. So why do we tolerate it when it comes to child care? Each of these elements is necessary in order for a child to get a fair chance in our society, to grow up to be a healthy, mature, responsible citizen.
So this Government has failed the challenge of child care. It has failed to bring in a program that is adequate to the need. Not only that, but it has brought in a program that will be producing fewer day care spaces than the existing program. So what it has produced is a fraud, a deception, a sleight of hand. It gives the impression through the headlines that it is taking bold action because you could read figures like $6.4 billion. But if you do a budgetary analysis, you will find it is in fact going to be spending less and creating fewer spaces than if it left things as they were.
The status quo is better than the Tory initiative. That is the sad reality of this day care package that is before this House. That is a tragedy for the children of this society. We would not tolerate a situation in which children did not have a school to go to. We would not tolerate a situation in which children did not have the health care that they needed. Why does this
Canada Child Care Act
Government ask Canadians to tolerate a situation in which children that need care do not have a child care program available for them? That is the question that this Government has to answer.
I want to sum up by saying that the Government has been shrewd and clever in its management of the news, in its management of the headlines. But when it comes down to the substance, when it comes down to meeting the human needs, it has failed. It has failed to meet the need. In fact, it has done less than what would have been done if it had left things alone. That is a sad commentary but an understandable one.
We know that it is the objective of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to cut back on social spending. He has indicated that in so many ways in so many areas of social policy. So this day care initiative fits with the objectives of the Minister of Finance, but it does not fit with the children of Canada, with the families of Canada. It fails abysmally, because it does not provide for what is needed. Not only that, but it reduces the commitment of the federal Government in the area of child care.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some very brief comments and put a question to my colleague. First of all, I would just like to comment slightly by saying that I think people listening tonight will find it a bit incredible that the Hon. Member would even indicate that what the Government is proposing today in terms of a day care policy is worse than the status quo when in fact it is investing $6.7 billion.
It does not require me to yell or to use great rhetoric to put that point across. Canadians listening to us tonight must know that any Government who spends $6.7 billion over a seven-year period, whether it is day care or anything else, is spending a lot of money-taxpayers' money.
It could be less.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
To just discard the policy, whether it is on day care or anything else, on such an issue is a challenge to the mind. How anybody could get up in the House of Commons and so blatantly push away such a policy is just incredible, it is a challenge to the mind. But then again, I guess if you are from the NDP, such challenges once in a while creep up and occur.
The question I want to put to the Hon. Member is of great interest to provincial governments, and to the provincial Government of the Province of Quebec. I know it is of some concern and I know also that the Members and their Party as well as the official critic have been saying that this legislation lacks in specifics on national norms, and it is their position that the legislation should include something very precise on that very issue. I want to know from the New Democratic Party of

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Canada how far they are ready to go in implementing what they thing should be national norms. The provincial Governments would certainly like to know.

Mr. Speaker, I must say I welcome my colleague's question. He makes the point that I made when I opened my speech. He said it is incredible that a Government that spends $6.4 billion is worse than the status quo. Well, on first blush, he makes sense in what he is saying. That is where the challenge comes in. The thing is, you just do not take a look at $6.4 billion in a vacuum. You have to compare it to what present government expenditures are and what are present government plans and programs for spending in the future. When you compare it on that level, what is revealed, once you pull away this curtain, is that in fact the new program will produce fewer day care spaces than the existing federal government programs. That is the interesting reality. People should get a chance to understand those facts.
I think that the Government's play for the headlines is not going to work as a political gambit. This is the first thing. The second thing was how far we would go with regard to national mores, which is what I think the Member said. Well, what we believe in this Party is that, when you establish a national social program such as day care, you must have national objectives. A responsible Government will say that this is the kind of program that we want, this is the kind of program that will provide for the day care needs and the child care needs of the nation. Then, of course, provinces can buy into the program and become involved.
First of all, you have to have the political leadership out of this Chamber and you have to have some accountability for those funds, accountability in terms of a national objective. The sad part of this program is that it is a program that gives no national direction. It turns over a pot of money to the provinces. It gives a global funding arrangement by which provinces can do whatever they want with the money, obviously in the day care field, but they can still do whatever they want. It is a hands-off approach, Mr. Speaker. It is the nightmare of Meech Lake. Rather than use the opportunity for political leadership and the opportunity to provide some direction, it takes a hands-off approach and says that the provinces can do whatever they want.
I disagree with our Liberal colleague who spoke earlier and who blamed this on the Meech Lake Accord. I would not blame it on the Meech Lake Accord. Given the Meech Lake Accord, you must have political leadership at the national level in order to provide direction so that you can have good national programs. If the federal Government had taken this approach when it came to the establishment of medicare, we would not have medicare in this country. I say to my colleague that we need to have national objectives. Then we will have set standards whereby the provincial Governments and the federal administration can be held accountable for the expenditures of those moneys according to the national objectives.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext: I have a very short supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I think Canadians from the Province of Quebec will find it of particular interest that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) from the New Democratic Party would describe this piece of legislation-if I heard him correctly-as the nightmare of Meech Lake. I want to know from him whether he intends, along with the Leader of his Party, because we are approaching a federal election in the next few months to a year, to enter the Province of Quebec and campaign specifically on that issue with regard to this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, all I would say is that you can have a Meech Lake nightmare and you can also have a Meech Lake dream. This Government has chosen the nightmare. It has chosen not to provide political leadership. If you want to have a dream, you have to provide leadership and direction. That is possible under our Constitution. The nightmare in this situation is that the Government has abdicated its responsibility to provide political leadership. The Government is abusing the Meech Lake Accord in that way. It is saying: "Okay, we will leave direction for day care to the provinces and we will provide no national leadership".

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to comment. The Minister of State for Youth and for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Charest) works within the ambit of the Department of National Health and Welfare. We understand why he is putting in a good word for his boss, the Minister. I must say that my colleague labelled this the "Epp plan" and then later on called it a fraud and deception. Members will appreciate that I might have felt those observations rather keenly.
Oh, oh!

If you allow me a moment or two, Mr. Speaker, to get precisely to the point, I would like to remind Canadians that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) in early 1985 published a paper on child benefits in which he promised that there would not be a reduction in child benefits and if there were in any part of that, the money would stay within the envelope, in the jargon of the federal Government, so it would not be lost to families. The same Minister was forced by September, 1985, to concede that there would be through deindexation of the family allowance, a reduction in child benefits which would be a loss to families because he would not, in fact, keep the money in his area of spending. He made no particular apology for having taken up the imperatives of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and, in the process, broke his word to Canadian families.
Though I might at first be inclined to feeling a little piqued at this harsh description of the "Epp plan" on child care, those Canadians who are watching and wondering whether my friend is telling the truth about a plan that can represent over the next seven years less spending if it is put into effect than
August 11, 1988

would occur if the existing arrangements under the Canada Assistance Plan, dating from the mid-1960s remain in effect, and if provinces take up the opportunity to provide child care under that joint funding arrangement between Ottawa and the provincial Governments of this country, it is possible.
My colleague says that this could be less spending, even if the Minister who has been commenting cannot believe that and finds it too much for his mind, but I must say that in working with youth he should be capable of understanding almost anything. The possibility that a Minister in the Conservative Government, as my friend has said very rightly, might be involved in just this kind of fraudulent game on the Canadian public seems to me quite possible, given the record of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He has yielded to Tuxedo and River Heights before against the interest of Steinbach and Ste. Anne, and he has done it one more time.

Mr. Speaker, when I spoke about the "Epp plan", obviously I was thinking more of Jake than of Ernie. When I said that it was a deception, I really was not trying to say that it was a "dis-Epp-tion". I was trying to say that it seemed to me to be misleading. I hope that I have not insulted my colleague. I certainly stand by my critique of the day care program of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, earlier I said to my colleague from the New Democratic Party that we had trouble sitting here listening to one of their speeches that contained, substantially, the following statement. The New Democratic Party tells us that this program worth $6 ...
. . . $6.4 billion . . .

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
. . . $6.4 billion which will be spent over a period of about seven years is peanuts. They would prefer to
Canada Child Care Act
keep the status quo. They would rather turn back the clock. They would rather not spend $6.4 billion in taxpayer's money.
If that is any indication of what we can expect during the next election campaign, there will not be much to fear. This is what is referred to in Quebec as the "Capitaine Bonhomme" technique. "Capitaine Bonhomme" used to say, and we even heard it said by the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin) when he was sitting with the NPD, when he shouted from the other side of the House that "les sceptiques seraient confondus"... Well, "Capitaine Bonhomme" seems to be in charge of the New Democratic Party's campaign committee.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of reasons why the Government decided to introduce this Bill and this policy. Today, we are specifically considering the Bill, but there is also a general strategy of which this Bill is a part. In recent years, there were a number of developments in our society that made our Government decide to react. These are developments that in fact all political parties are able to recongnize. We agree on that. There is for instance the fact, and this has already been mentioned, that women are entering the labour market in increasing numbers. It is not for us to judge whether it is a good or a bad thing. It is a fact of life. I think it is a good thing. I think women have the right to do so just as men did before. People no longer question their right to enter the labour market, and if they make that choice, just as men make the same choice, they should be allowed to do so.
So this is one factor making child care services increasingly important. There are other factors besides, Mr. Speaker. Family structure in our society has changed, for all sorts of reasons, good or bad; again, we are not to judge that today, but, for example, there are more and more single-parent families. So there are more and more women who are single mothers with children and who have to take care of them and at the same time earn their living; they must work. The children must still be cared for. These women, like so many others, do not make much money and child care services are important-that is another important factor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
speechtext: The NDP does not understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
My colleague from Champlain (Mr. Champagne) says that the New Democratic Party does not understand that. I would not have said that, Mr. Speaker, but I tend to agree with him. I did not say it.
So, Mr. Speaker, added to that, and I think that we have not talked much about the changes within the labour market itself... We tend to think these days that in this modern era, investment, modernization and all that will bring jobs. Whenever we announce subsidies, for example, we try to help companies in the regions through regional economic development. From time to time, we automatically think that this means jobs. That is not always true, Mr. Speaker. You know, investing and modernizing sometimes mean loss of employment and it is difficult to put that in context. But we modernize to be more competitive.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Canada is an exporting country, and it is probably one of the few countries in the world that depends to such a great extent on exports as a percentage of its gross domestic product. There is also West Germany, and in fact we are both very close. Since Canada is an exporting country, we have to invest and we have to be competitive as a country, and sometimes that means losing jobs. All that to reach a simple conclusion! This means that changes in the labour market are important. For instance, the number of jobs in the service sector in Canada is increasing. In the forties, about 40 per cent of jobs were in the service industry in this country, while by 1986, it was 75 per cent. What this means? Well traditionally, women are more highly represented in the service sector than they are in any other industry. Ironically, and I say ironically in referring to the last two years, women have performed well on the labour market because of shifts in the kind of jobs available. Such shifts are not unique to Canada. They are a worldwide phenomenon. It means more and more part-time work, sometimes temporary work, which is another facet of the situation of women on the labour market and in fact of whole families.
Mr. Speaker, one aspect that has not been discussed today is the role played by men, because in recent years, the emphasis has been on discussing what the role of women should be in the family, on the labour market and so forth, but men are also changing the way they live. Men enter the labour market, their jobs change, they are displaced by new technology, and they are asked to play an increasingly important role in terms of society's values with respect to men. I noticed in the course of this debate that there have been very few references to the changing roles of men, and I know something about the subject. The Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) knows about this and the Hon. Member for Chambly (Mr. Grise) as well. We have young families, we have young children and all that, and our roles are changing as well. There is another person who is knowledgeable on the subject, Mr. Speaker, and I am proud to refer to our Prime Minister.
He changes diapers.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
He is very close to his family, and Members on both sides of the House have seen for themselves that he is very much attached to his family and his wife. It is a marvelous sight. People think he is promoting certain values, but he is also keenly aware, and I have discussed the matter with him, of the fact that men have to change their attitudes within the family unit. It's all very well to put all the mechanisms in place, but men will have to do more. They will have to redefine and share to a greater extent the responsibilities within the family unit.
That being said, it is clear, Mr. Speaker, that we need more day care. We need more day care so that these people can live, can develop and participate fully in the labour market and in
Canadian society, because that is what we mean by participation in our society.
I see the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) who is joining us. Please sit down and join us! It's nice to see you again. So the Hon. Member for Outremont is with us again, and I am delighted to see her, because I have some comments and questions. However, we all agree that these needs exist and that these changes are taking place. We are probably more sensitive to the changing roles of men in our Party, since the other parties never even mentioned the subject. We decided to talk about it this evening. There is a problem, however, when we talk about the means for bringing about these changes.
Members of the New Democratic Party have already told us what they thought of our approach. We intend to spend $6.7 billion, and their answer was that it was peanuts, did not mean a thing and was regressive. I would like to know how many people are sitting in Sherbrooke this evening in that beautiful riding of mine who are going to believe that. These are people who already pay taxes every Thursday. Just imagine, their paycheck arrives, part of it is taken away, and the New Democratic Party tells them that $6.7 billion is peanuts! They want to take the rest of your paycheck as well! What really worries me is that they are going to deduct so much income tax from my constituents' paychecks in the riding of Sherbrooke that they will not be able to afford the day care the Government wants to give them. In any case, that is another problem.
As far as the practical side is concerned, the Government wanted to establish a policy that would respect the jurisdiction of the provinces, because after all we are in Canada and not in the United States or Great Britain. Policies are not developed in a vacuum. They evolve within the constitutional reality of this country which provides that the provinces have certain jurisdictions. And the Province of Quebec, and this should be of interest to the Hon. Member for Outremont, also has its own jurisdiction. If we discuss the matter with our counterparts in Quebec, I am sure they would be interested to talk to you about their jurisdiction.
In the Bill before the House today, Mr. Speaker, we appreciate that reality and we want to make certain adjustments. The New Democratic Party and the federal Liberal Party of Canada do not recognize that reality. I know that. I have already heard what they had to say in the House. They claim, for instance, that we are not setting national standards and are not showing any leadership.
Mr. Speaker, let's be honest. What they are saying is totally false.
They did nothing for twenty years!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
We have to call a spade a spade. It's just not true.
August 11, 1988

The Bill contains some very clear indications in that respect. The standards that we ask the provinces to develop and implement include (1) the child:care-giver ratio; (2) the qualifications of the day care staff; (3) the size of the groups by age and type of care; (4) health and safety measures; and the nature of parental participation, Mr. Speaker. What we plan to enforce those standards, Mr. Speaker, is specific agreements with the provinces recognizing, for example, that Quebec may be more advanced than the other provinces. Are you going to deny that? You see, they almost agree with us. I am sure that the Hon. Member for Outremont will vote for the Bill at this rate.
Are Quebec and Ontario, for example, as advanced as other provinces like New Brunswick, for example? Are they as advanced in New Brunswick as in Ontario, Mr. Speaker? To ask the question is to answer it. Basically, what is wrong with a Bill that recognizes these realities? Do we always have to act as if that were not the case or must we, the federal Government, always impose our will on everything? It is not necessary, Mr. Speaker, when you want to do things that work, practical things out in the field. When the time comes to act, when choices have to be made, when you have to implement what was discussed, be it in 15 or 20 years when they were in power or in our case, in the space of one mandate, the reasonable time we took to put this together, when that time comes, these realities must be recognized. Something must be done for those people. That is exactly what this Bill does.
There are three main objectives. Our national policy can also be divided into three parts, more or less. First, what we are trying to do, looking at the objectives as a whole, is to develop a flexible strategy, one that respects the parents' right to choose. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, we as a party-this may surprise you because I know ... Not you, excuse me, it will not surprise you. We have great respect for your intelligence, Mr. Speaker, but it surprises the people on the other side, both in the federal Liberal Party and in the New Democratic Party. Imagine that-we want to let parents choose. What a sin! What a scandal to presume that Canadians can have the intelligence to choose what to do with their own tax money! We will have a choice soon, Mr. Speaker, you see, because another Government would take their money and tell them that is the way it is. Not only will they take your money, they will take twice as much. We will take twice as much, as the New Democratic Party would say, and we will give you no choice because we know what is good for you.
Mr. Speaker, we believe we are past that stage. Because people are intelligent. Earlier they referred to the fact I am Minister of State (Youth). True, I am the Minister of State (Youth), but I do not claim I know our young people very well, in the sense that I do not know each choice of each individual. But I know them well enough to know that they want to have a choice, they want to make their own choice. They want to be treated as full partners in our Canadian society.
The legislation recognizes that reality.
Canada Child Care Act
We also want to ensure that child care is accessible, affordable, and of better quality. This is what we are aiming at.
So this Government uses three major approaches. There is increased tax assistance to families, Mr. Speaker-this is the first approach, an important approach that will put some money into their pockets through the tax system. The second approach is the new fund for child care project implementation, and there you will see a certain diversity in the approaches taken, recognizing the fact there is no magic solution, no uniform solution for everyone, and what we aim to do through that new fund, Mr. Speaker, is for instance to give an opportunity to those who want to offer specialized services, to submit project proposals.
As I am speaking, Mr. Speaker, this Government is accepting projects, examining them through National Health and Welfare, in order that a group wanting to have a project for handicapped children in a child care centre can do so. It is important to be able to recognize those differences. This is what we mean when we refer to the right of choice. Because not all people are alike. We cannot have a ready-made system that will fit everyone because there are for instance ethnic groups, and they can chose to submit a special project.
Groups with handicapped children for instance can make that choice. There are all kinds of reasons, all kinds of differences that make our society richer in all kinds of ways, and this we would like to recognize through that program.
Through the legislation indeed. Of course, the legislation now before us.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me offer a remark that goes a little beyond the subject at hand this evening, but that is directly linked to the legislation and the result expected from this legislation. The question we must ask now as we sit in this House, after the decision taken by the Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada (Mr. Turner) is this: Will he or will he not instruct the Senate to block this legislation?
Because as you see, Mr. Speaker, the votes of Canadian men and women is not good enough any more. Because if today you are a federal Liberal, Mr. Speaker, you can decide what is good or what is bad, no matter how the people voted. The vote of each Canadian man and woman has been reduced, diminished that very day the Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada (Mr. Turner) stooped himself to block Government legislation in the Senate, on free trade of course. That is what I am talking about. Even though he promised to tear up the deal as soon as he would be elected leader of this country, he changes his mind, he turns around, and claims that no, a non-elected Senate does have the right and will be asked to show its expertise in filibustering.
In other words, in order to protect, and it is a real challenge to understand the reasoning behind this whole thing, Mr. Speaker, in order to protect democracy, John Turner decides to deny democracy. That is the new philosophy of the federal Liberal Party. You've got to see it to believe it! A few months ago, this same man, Mr. Speaker, while being stabbed in the

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
back by half the members of his own caucus, was referring to the democratic process by which he was elected. In 1986, more than half the members of his caucus told him to quit and leave his Party and stabbed him in the back. And where was he during all this time? We know! He was going through a very difficult time, a very painful family ordeal, while half of his caucus, more than half of his caucus were democratically stabbing him in the back and telling him to quit. And what did John Turner say? Democracy, my friends! In November 1986, 76 per cent of our delegates elected me leader of the Party. I have the right to retain my position, based on the democratic fundamental principle of our country. Now, a few months later, he changes his mind and says: Let us forget about democracy! The non-elected Liberal Senate can now start filibustering.
Mr. Speaker, I only mention this because in a few months Canadians will have the opportunity to vote, and, in fact, to make a big decision. They will have to determine the value of their vote for all subsequent elections. If the strategy used by the Canadian Senate, and by the federal Liberal Party of Canada, ever succeeds, from that time on, the value of the voting right of each and every Canadian will be diminished, and a Bill like this one would be jeopardized by a leader as weak as John Turner, and a party as weak and as undemocratic as the federal Liberal Party of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin).

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of State for Youth who seems to know everything about day care centres ... in fact, he seems to know a lot of things. He made a case for day care centres by referring to the Senate and the Liberal Party.
I wish he would give me more details because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has had a lot to say about the war his Governement is waging against drugs and cocaine. As it happens, one preventive program against juvenile delinquency would involve extracurricular day care centres for children aged 6 to 14. We also know that 57 per cent of these children are alone after school hours.
Since he mentioned the Province of Quebec I am telling him that it is one of the crucial problems facing Quebec-I mean extracurricular centres-because it is the only province which makes grants to support this kind of day care centres.
So what does his Government intend to do to promote day care centres, because there is no reference to them in the legislation? Clause 2 even excludes services relating to education.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) should ask me that question, particularly as it relates to Quebec and fields of jurisdiction.
We on this side are somewhat taken aback by the statements made by the federal Liberal Party of Canada, especially by her colleague the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) and by herself, the Hon. Member for Outremont, to the effect that the legislation fails to give a clear definition of the standards, that the standards are not clear enough.
What I would like to know is just how far the federal Liberal Party of Canada is prepared to go to impose these standards and how far it is prepared to go to impose them within the Province of Quebec.
Can the Hon. Member for Outremont tell us whether she knows the answer to that question, because I would like to know. I would like to know what they will tell Quebecers about the standards.
Mr. Speaker, in response to her question, she knows full well that the legislation provides for agreements. I can tell you that our objective is to be as flexible as possible so that we will be able to acknowledge the legitimate options of the provinces while taking into consideration their needs and, if you will, how far they have progressed in the day care sector.
Still the Hon. Member for Outremont ought to be able to tell us whether or not the Liberal Party of Quebec is at one with the federal Liberal Party of Canada when it comes to the question of standards. Do they agree with them, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and I want to direct a question to the Minister. My comment is that his speech was excellent in its rhetoric but a failure in its substance. He seemed afraid to answer questions. He was afraid to answer the question of the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin). Therefore, I want to ask him a question.
As I understand it, the Meech Lake Accord permits establishment of national objectives for new social programs which the federal Government funds. Child care is a new social program which the federal Government is funding. Why did the Government not put in place standards for the provinces? The provinces are getting all this money and are essentially going to set up child care.
I have a further question for the Minister and I would ask him to answer it. Does he believe that the federal Government should set up standards when it gives money like this to the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing at this time the old school of thought of the NDP, the New Democratic Party of the late 1980s versus the early 1980s New Democratic Party of Canada, the one that voted with the federal Liberal Party to repatriate the Constitution even though the Quebec National Assembly had voted unanimously against that. There are two schools of thought in the New Democratic Party. We heard one of them tonight and at this point in time are witnessing the other school of thought.
August 11, 1988

The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has expressed his opposition to the Meech Lake Accord with some conviction and has paid a price for that. He is asking us, in the context of his personal opposition, which is not consistent with the position of his own Party, for our answer on the question of national norms.
The first answer is obvious although it may not be obvious to the Hon. Member. I say that respectfully because the Hon. Member operates on a centralized premise. He sees Canada as having a centralized government. The fact is that there are different jurisdictions in Canada. This legislation recognizes those different jurisdictions. There should be nothing surprising about the fact that the provinces have jurisdiction in this.
Through this legislation we recognize the specific areas in which the federal Government, with the provinces, wants to establish some norms including the ratio between children and those who keep them; the qualifications of the personnel; the sizes of the groups, their ages and types; regulations on health and security; and the nature of parental participation. These are all things provided for in the legislation and they should be consistent with the way in which Canada operates.

speechtext: Questions and comments are now over. On debate, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) has the floor.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the Minister is delighted to see that the question and comment period is over. He has nearly lost his voice from so much shouting. It is to be feared that if he should continue like this, he could choke again, Mr. Speaker.
I do not think there is a single Member in this House who is now fully aware of just how important this debate on Bill C-144 is. I am one of those who would like to emphasize the impact this Bill is likely to have on their ridings and, if I may, I should like to refer to a survey which was carried out not so long ago on this issue in my own riding and share with my colleagues its findings.
But before coming to the heart of the matter, I should like first of all to state unequivocally that the needs do exist. It is a well established fact. Several commissions of inquiry have already made a number of recommendations, the issue has been thorougly examined, so that the time now is for action and not for further studies.

I do not think there is any argument on the need for an increase in adequate child care spaces in Canada. That has been fully explained and documented over the years, as far back as the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in 1970.
I want to put on the record a statement made by my leader on October 26, 1986. At that time he stated on The Nation's Business'.
"We in the Liberal Party believe that any child care system must be based on two principles: 1) sharing the burden and 2) providing choices.
Our proposal is that parents, the private sector, and provincial and federal governments will share the costs. It will be a mixed program, with more facilities and help for those who do not have access to the facilities- particularly in rural areas."

Mr. Speaker, several Members of this House have clearly demonstrated today that child care has become a social issue. Canadian families have experienced dramatic changes over the

August U, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
past twenty years as a result of an increasing shift in population towards urban areas in an effort to adapt to a more modern way of life. Things have changed gradually so that now traditional families with only one bread winner are now a minority and we see more and more the advent of new families structures. Take, for instance, the case of single parent families. They represent 20 per cent of all the families in my riding; in other words, one in every five families is a single parent family and 90 per cent of them with children. Nowadays, there are childless couples, families with two bread winners, families which are entirely different from those which existed 25 or 30 years ago, and we must create the social structures to meet the important challenge we are faced with in 1988, namely, how to deal with the children, and especially those who need day care because both their parents are part of the labour force.
Thanks to a questionnaire which I circulated in my riding a few months ago, I came to the realization that a great many of my constituents are very much interested in this issue.
According to Statistics Canada's most recent report, there are 19,265 families in my constituency. Of that number, 8,180 do not have children at home and 3,635 are single-parent families, including 3,075 headed by women. There is a total of 18,520 children at home, including 4,325 aged six years or less. They are the ones needing day care services.
Besides the changes I was talking about earlier, there is a large increase in the number of women in the workforce, particularly those with children under six. In 1967, 16 per cent of those women were in the workforce whereas now, 20 years later, that number is 56 per cent among women with children aged three years or less and 63 per cent among those with children between three and five. It is a radical change.
Therefore, we see right away that something must be done to help those women and families take care of their children because it is the next generation of Canadians that is at stake.
Mr. Speaker, it is essentially the economic conditions which caused the changes I was talking about. Since 1960, the purchasing power of single-income families has not stopped decreasing. That has put more and more pressure on those families and forced many of their members to work outside the home. The reality is that 44 per cent of Canadian families now rely on both spouses to bring home the money required to support the household. It is a reality that we, as responsible lawmakers, must take into account.
For millions of children currently needing day care services because both their parents are in the workforce, there are only
250,000	spaces in public child care centres, which barely meet 15 per cent of the demand. It is not enough, we know it, something must be done.
Because there are not enough spaces in day care centres children must put up with day care services of lesser quality, constantly change sitters or, worse, be kept under the care of persons whose qualifications are doubtful if not inexistent.
That, Mr. Speaker, is not what we consider as adequate in many cases.
Parents who have been able to find acceptable day care services still have a problem: professional services cost a great deal. One must be ready to pay between $4,000 and $6,000 a year per child.
As an example, I was discussing this problem some time ago with my parliamentary assistant whose wife works outside the home. They have two children. They are among those in my riding who have been able to find a quality day care centre. They are satisfied with the quality of service provided at the centres their two children go to.
However, that couple must pay $500 a month for the four-year old child and more than $800 a month for the one-year-old. That amounts to more than $1,300 a month for the two children, or $15,600 a year for the assistant of a Member of Parliament who is not paid a high salary. Unfortunately, we cannot pay our assistants as much as we would like to, we are on a tight budget, but I know that in order to pay $15,600 a year of family income for day care this individual is making sacrifices. Mr. Speaker, those parents tried for a while to answer their need for day care but economic conditions are getting too much for them. Considering the amounts I have just cited, we can see how much more difficult to solve my assistant's problem can be for other low or middle income Canadian families.
Day care services will therefore be restricted more and more to an elite who can afford to pay what they cost. That is not what we mean when we talk about reforming the system, giving Canadians the day care services they need.
We can see it is urgent to solve the problem. But the need to act does not mean forsaking the opportunity to review the problems to be solved and the ways to solve them.
Mr. Speaker, I think that there are two ways that the Government tries to help families with children and we know that for many years, billions of dollars have been spent to help Canadian families meet their needs.
Mr. Speaker, we now spend $5 billion a year through the tax system to help Canadian families with children. First, there are government benefits for families with children. These families enjoy several programs collectively known as the Child Benefits Plan. They are family allowances, the child tax credit and the tax exemption for dependent children.
In 1984-85, net expenditures for the Child Benefits Plan were $4.09 billion and it is estimated that in 1986, $4.82 billion was spent on this budget item.
The other aspect is child care services. In addition to government financial support for child care, this service takes four forms: (1) the income tax deduction for child care expenses; (2) sharing the cost of subsidized child care services for low-income families with the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan, which has existed for many years, as we know.
August 11, 1988

When I hear my colleagues from the Government side say that the previous Government never did anything . . . They cannot be serious, because for many years, there have been both tax programs and direct assistance programs to help Canadian families meet their needs to raise children.
Third are the training allowances for parents taking courses sponsored by Employment and Immigration Canada.
It is well known today that training programs are available to Canadian men and women and that if they need child care services, the federal Government provides financial contributions to that end.
Fourth, there are contributions by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development for child care services and Day care services in Indian reserves. Those four measures have cost about 224 millions dollars in 1984, according to the last figures available.
Those amounts seem high at first, but one must not forget that the deduction for child care expenses benefits primarily high revenue families and only if they can provide receipts. That as is very important!
As we have seen earlier, those who can afford to pay more than 1,000 $ a month in child care expenses are entitled to a tax break, but not those who have inadequate or almost nonexistent revenues.
Assistance is provided to low revenue families through the Cost Sharing Program of the Public Assistance Program of Canada, but less than 20 per cent of eligible children six years old or less have benefited from this program up to now.
Furthermore, some measures allow families to raise their children. There are the family allowances which have been in existence for many years, as well as the child tax credit, the tax deduction for children. Unfortunately, all those have been reduced, Mr. Speaker. They have been reduced by the Mulroney Government through desindexation.
This has had a serious impact on poor and low income families. According to figures available to us, every family will lose ground in 1990 with the deindexation of those tax measures.
The situation is therefore urgent. It has to be dealt with. We, in the Liberal party, believe in the major principles which must underlie this reform of assistance to child care services. So, before dealing with the Government Bill, that is C-144, I want to recall the principles stated in several reports, but more recently in the minority report presented to the committee by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin), entitled Choices for Child Care: Now and in the Future, dated March 1987. Mr. Speaker, this document has to be read, for it represents a serious approach and gives an alternative which could in my opinion provide us with a good solution.
Canada Child Care Act
First of all, we believe in the value of the parents' role. In order for them to be able to care for their children, we have to create programs of parental leave, flexible working hours, work sharing, etc. It is difficult, I grant you that, but it is not impossible. We will have to use our imagination, innovate a little, but that is the challenge we are facing in the workplace today. As we know, more and more businesses and industries provide and must continue to provide day care services, because that may be the solution to some of the problems.
Second, we need quality services which will guarantee the full development of the children. Child care is not a mere physical surveillance. These children are the next generation of citizens and the services we provide must prepare them to achieve their full development. In that respect, the school system is the most elaborate and valued child care system we have. The youngest should not, because of their age, be neglected. Young children are young human beings and they have the right to be treated as such. To that end, we will have to set and enforce basic standards dealing with accommodation, programs and staff training to ensure a good emotional, intellectual and social development of our children.
The third main principle is the development of institutions to implement over the years a comprehensive child care system of good quality, everywhere in Canada.
Fourth, there is the important principle of justice and equity. What does it mean? It means that assistance must go to the families most in need and that all families in the same situation must share the same opportunities.
The fifth objective is social justice, which means that the cost of child care must be shared equally among beneficiaries, namely governments, parents and employers.
The sixth objective is the harmonization of programs between provinces. I touched on a similar aspect a few minutes ago when I talked about the principle of equity between families. We think that all Canadians must have access to the same or a comparable level of service throughout the country, regardless of their province of residence. We will always object to a double or triple standard within Canada. There must be national standards for child care services as there are for health services. It is absolutely essential.
Lastly, there is the question of fiscal accountability. We saw that the amounts involved are very substantial. We are talking several billion dollars. Therefore, it is essential that there be some kind of accountability to ensure that the funds provided to provinces are used according to the objectives set by the federal government. I believe in the sharing of powers between the various jurisdictions. However, since child care services is a federal initiative funded by the federal Government, it seems to me that it is just common sense that there be some kind of accountability for those programs.

August 11, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Mr. Speaker, those were the objectives that we, Liberals, want to have included in any legislation on child care. And not only the Liberals favour them, Mr. Speaker, but Canadian people do too. As I said earlier, I polled the constituents in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier on this issue. The responses I got confirm what I just said. Out of 1,404 people who answered, 1,192 or 85 per cent think that the parents should pay all or part of the child care expenses, which brings forward the matter of social responsibility that I mentioned earlier.
As well, 33 per cent believe that the system should be universal and 56 per cent stated that such a program should only be offered to families in need. Moreover 59 per cent of the people in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier favor a system of funding based on revenues supplemented by some form of government assistance. This is what I was talking about when speaking of new trends in the workplace. Fifty per cent of the respondents favour child care services at the workplace.
In my riding, people agree with the establishment of child care services, but they remain realistic and believe in family responsibility, in a fair funding of child care and in helping families in need. As for us, we endorse those objectives and believe furthermore that any family in need should have access to the best child care services which should be offered according to the paying capacity of theses families.
Mr. Speaker, when looking at the Government proposal to solve this problem, we realize that the Tories have once again missed the boat. As I have said, the main problem is the lack of spaces since only 15 per cent of the needs are presently fulfilled. Some two millions additionnal places ought to be created. However, the government wishes to respond to the problem mainly with tax credits.
With a $6.4 billion budget over seven years, they intend to allocate a little less than $4 billion in cost-sharing programs with the provinces towards the creation of additional spaces.
Mr. Speaker, a refundable tax credit is contrary to the principle of a fair family treatment since every family will be getting $200 more over two years, going from $500 to $700, no matter what their needs are and whether they in fact spend that sum on child care. Tax credit will in no way contribute to the creation of new spaces, while funds targetted for the creation of new spaces will be too scarce to allow for a universal access to child care services.
The number of profitable child care services will increase as a result of Bill C-144 which will provide families with more money for day care while not contributing the necessary funds to create additional spaces in public or non profit organizations.
Mr. Speaker, this is the kind of approach the Governement has chosen to take. I doubt it is the right one, but it is its choice having been elected to govern. The Government has failed to show leadership in that area. I blame it for that. But is not the first time it surrenders its national responsibilities.
The issue of national standards which was mentionned earlier and discussed on many occasions before, is a fondamen-tal issue since the federal Government must maintain some kind of parity between various programs under different jurisdictions as a result of its constitutionnal or financial involvment.
Canadians are entitled to the same services wherever they live in Canada. That is a fundamental point, a matter of justice and fairness, and the Government is to be blamed for not having established national standards in this legislation. He is introducing a bill on child care . . .
